SA exporters face Agoa setback, but broader US trade ties remain intact
While the loss of preferential access could put thousands of jobs at risk, the economic consequences are manageable if government and business work together to identify alternative markets and trade opportunities, says NWU Business School economist, Raymond Parsons.
He argues that the development should serve as a catalyst for accelerating export diversification, strengthening regional and international trade partnerships and improving South Africa’s global competitiveness.
"Although the loss of Agoa preferences is highly regrettable and the specific sectoral impact may be painful, the situation is manageable if the right market adaptations are made," Parsons says. "Addressing the negative economic consequences of losing Agoa preferences will therefore continue to require close collaboration between government and the relevant business interests to identify alternative trade strategies."
Despite the Agoa decision, non-Agoa trade relations with the US remain far more substantial, with the overwhelming bulk of SA’s exports to that country falling outside Agoa preferences, Parsons says.
"This trade then drives the vast majority of existing bilateral economic ties between SA and the US. The non-Agoa trade relationships are therefore reinforced by a robust footprint that goes beyond trade balances. The Agoa result still means that the core economic pipeline of trade and investment connecting SA and the US remains intact, and must continue to be nurtured."
Adapting to trade shifts
Nevertheless, Parsons says the exclusion reinforces two priorities for South Africa.
"First, SA must accelerate its market diversification strategy in a changing geoeconomic world that offers new opportunities. Enlarging and diversifying trade options includes expanding East Asian market access to growing economies there, as well as further leveraging economic opportunities through the African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA)," Parsons notes.
"Secondly, the government must aim to make the domestic economy more internationally competitive by reducing the costs of doing business in SA. This in particular encompasses expediting logistics reform, especially in rail and port facilities, that will help to offset the Agoa loss by keeping SA globally competitive.
"Ultimately, South Africa's ability to absorb the impact of losing Agoa preferences will depend less on the loss itself than on how quickly it adapts," Parsons adds.
He argues that diversifying export markets, strengthening trade partnerships and addressing domestic competitiveness constraints will be essential to keeping exporters globally competitive and sustaining the country's broader trade and investment relationships.

US terminates AGOA access for Rwanda and South Africa
The United States government has announced its intention to terminate the trade preference status of Rwanda and South Africa under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a move that will strip both nations of duty-free access to the American market starting January 1, 2027.
US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer confirmed President Donald Trump’s decision, stating that the administrations in Pretoria and Kigali are engaging in practices that violate the eligibility requirements of the landmark trade programme. The termination shuts the two African economies out of preferential access to the US market, marking one of the most significant diplomatic and economic ruptures between Washington and sub-Saharan Africa in recent years.
AGOA, enacted in 2000, has long served as the cornerstone of US economic engagement with Africa, allowing eligible sub-Saharan countries to export thousands of products duty-free to the United States. To maintain this status, beneficiary nations must meet strict criteria, including establishing market-based economies, the rule of law, political pluralism, and the elimination of barriers to US trade and investment. They must also protect human rights and avoid activities that undermine US national security or foreign policy interests.
Legal mechanisms and diplomatic friction
The legal mechanism for this expulsion relies on the executive authority granted to the US President under the original AGOA legislation. The law explicitly requires the President to monitor the progress of beneficiary countries and empowers the executive to withdraw designation if a country is not making continual progress in meeting the eligibility criteria. By formally declaring that both nations are engaging in inconsistent practices, Ambassador Greer has initiated the statutory withdrawal process, which mandates a consultation period with the US Congress before the termination becomes irrevocable.
While the US government has not released an exhaustive public dossier detailing every infraction, the Trump administration’s concerns regarding Rwanda primarily centre on human rights abuses and restrictions on political freedom. Kigali has faced sustained criticism from international rights organisations over the suppression of political opposition and the alleged transnational repression of dissidents.
For South Africa, the friction is largely rooted in its foreign policy alignments and trade disputes. Pretoria has drawn intense scrutiny from Washington over its diplomatic posture, particularly its relations with US geopolitical adversaries and its stance on various international conflicts. Furthermore, South Africa has faced ongoing trade irritants, including disputes over poultry tariffs and access for US agricultural producers, which Washington has repeatedly argued violate the spirit of AGOA’s market-access provisions.
Economic fallout for export sectors
The economic consequences of the expulsion will be immediate and severe for both nations once the January 2027 deadline takes effect. South Africa is arguably the most sophisticated beneficiary of AGOA, using the preferential access to build a robust export pipeline, particularly in the automotive and agricultural sectors. The automotive industry, which relies heavily on duty-free access to export vehicles to the US, faces the prospect of suddenly being subjected to standard Most Favoured Nation (MFN) tariffs. These standard tariffs could render South African exports uncompetitive against rivals in Asia and Latin America, threatening thousands of manufacturing jobs in the Eastern Cape and Gauteng provinces.
Furthermore, Pretoria’s agricultural sector, which has battled sanitary and phytosanitary barriers to export citrus and stone fruit to the US, now faces the additional burden of import duties. Industry bodies have warned that the combined effect of non-tariff barriers and the sudden imposition of tariffs could devastate commercial farming operations that have oriented their supply chains toward the North American market.
Rwanda, though a smaller economy, has leveraged AGOA to develop a burgeoning apparel and textile manufacturing sector. The loss of duty-free quotas will likely trigger factory closures and job losses in a country that has aggressively positioned itself as a light-manufacturing hub for the region. Kigali had previously engaged in trade disputes with Washington over second-hand clothing imports, which resulted in the temporary suspension of its apparel benefits, making the broader termination a compounding economic blow.
Strategic recalibration of US-Africa trade
The decision underscores a shift in US trade policy under the current administration, which has increasingly prioritised strict bilateral compliance and geopolitical alignment over the broad-based developmental goals that historically underpinned AGOA. By wielding the threat and eventual execution of AGOA expulsion as a foreign policy tool, Washington is signalling that trade preferences are conditional on broader diplomatic cooperation and adherence to American strategic interests.
Regional economic blocs and trade analysts are now assessing the potential contagion effect. The expulsion of two of the continent's most prominent economies raises questions about the future stability of AGOA, which is currently undergoing its periodic renewal debates in the US Congress. African trade negotiators have long argued for a more predictable, long-term renewal of the pact to encourage fixed capital investment, but the politicisation of eligibility criteria introduces a new layer of uncertainty for investors operating across the continent. This uncertainty complicates the objectives of the African Continental Free Trade Area, as external market shocks force nations to recalibrate their industrialisation strategies without guaranteed access to their most lucrative overseas markets.
Trade unions and civil society organisations in South Africa have expressed alarm at the potential job losses, urging the government to urgently repair diplomatic relations with Washington. The termination represents a profound recalibration of US-Africa economic relations, prioritising strategic compliance over historical trade solidarity, and leaves both Pretoria and Kigali with a narrow window to engage in high-level diplomatic interventions before the new year.

articles.title: Ethiopia: Will Renewed Conflict Derail Ethiopia's Economic Growth? - allAfrica.com
articles.summary: Ethiopia: Will Renewed Conflict Derail Ethiopia's Economic Growth?  allAfrica.com
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. But renewed fighting in the north of the BRICS member state could deter investment, strain public finances and push up the cost of living.
Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year. But renewed fighting in the north, high reconstruction costs and climate-related crop problems are threatening the country's economic recovery.
London-based financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the consequences of further escalation. "If there is a major conflict [...] the current economic growth will not be sustainable," he told DW.
The costly legacy of the Tigray war
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
The war that raged in Tigray and other parts of Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022 inflicted extensive damage. Infrastructure was destroyed, businesses lost production capacity and agricultural land could no longer be cultivated in some areas.
A World Bank-backed damage and needs assessment puts the damage caused by several conflicts in Ethiopia between November 2020 and December 2021 at more than $22.6 billion (€20.2 billion). Economic losses amounted to around $6 billion. The estimated bill for reconstruction and economic recovery stands at approximately $19.7 billion, which covers the total funding needed, not annual costs or damage caused by the current escalation.
A reconstruction plan covered the period from 2023 to 2028. However, it remains uncertain whether the work can be fully funded and completed within that timeframe.
Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed believes the economic consequences of the Tigray war were even more severe. In addition to the direct destruction, he points to lost economic output, high inflation and foreign currency shortages at the time. International trade conditions also deteriorated: in 2022, Ethiopia lost its benefits under the US African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which had allowed certain African exports to enter the US market duty-free.
Growth despite the crisis
Following the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022, the economy began to recover. According to the IMF, it grew by 7.2% in 2022–23 and 8.1% in 2023–24. The organization puts growth at 9.2% for 2024–25 and forecasts a further 9.2% for 2025–26. Agriculture, mining and electricity generation are among the main drivers.
This does not contradict the economic damage caused by the war. Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the total economic output of a country. If major sectors outside conflict-affected areas continue to expand, the overall economy can grow even while individual regions are still suffering the consequences of violence.
However, high growth rates do not mean that the country's economic problems have been resolved. Reconstruction remains a major challenge, inflation continues to put pressure on households and the government has to service its debt. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. Reforms supported by an IMF program launched in 2024 are intended to address structural weaknesses in the economy.
More military spending, less money for development
A renewed escalation could put additional pressure on public finances. The government would have to spend more on military personnel, equipment and logistics. At the same time, economic activity and, consequently, tax revenues could decline in the affected regions.
"A substantial share of government resources would be tied up in military spending that would otherwise be available for infrastructure, education and social services," warned Abdulmenan Mohammed. The extent of this impact would depend on the scale and duration of any renewed conflict.A prolonged war could also prompt businesses to postpone investments. International lenders and donors might become more cautious, while the government would need additional funds for security and humanitarian assistance. This could leave less money available for roads, energy infrastructure and other development projects.
Inflation and foreign currency shortages
The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7% for 2025–26. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising, although at a slower pace than in previous years.
Abdulmenan Mohammed expects a further escalation to intensify inflationary pressures. "If the conflict escalates further, inflation is likely to rise," he said. To finance additional spending, the government might resort to more domestic borrowing. This could crowd out private businesses by making it harder for them to access credit and finance investments.
The military also needs foreign currency to purchase equipment from abroad. If this demand increases, fewer foreign exchange reserves could be available to private businesses for imports. This would put further pressure on the birr exchange rate and drive up the cost of imported goods, fuel and industrial inputs.
The extent of these effects on the BRICS member state would also depend on export earnings, monetary policy and developments in international markets. A new surge in inflation is therefore a risk, but not an inevitable consequence of the escalation. A combination of rising prices and uncertain incomes would be particularly difficult for poorer households.
Agriculture and tourism particularly vulnerable
Abdulmenan Mohammed sees agriculture, as well as the tourism and hospitality sectors, as particularly vulnerable. "Agriculture is especially exposed because much of the fighting takes place in rural areas where farmers work," he said.
Insecurity around farmland, disrupted transport routes and shortages of agricultural inputs can undermine production. At the same time, parts of the country are experiencing insufficient rainfall and poor harvest prospects. Failed harvests reduce farmers' incomes, while lower food supplies can push prices even higher.
Tourism is also highly sensitive to security risks. Travel advisories and reports of fighting can deter visitors, reducing revenues for hotels and tour operators.
Could neighboring countries benefit from the crisis?
When making investment decisions, international investors consider not only market size but also political stability, security and the reliability of state institutions. A further escalation could therefore delay investment decisions or prompt companies to consider alternative locations.
However, there is currently no concrete evidence that companies are already withdrawing investments from Ethiopia because of the fighting and relocating them to neighboring countries such as Kenya. Abdulmenan Mohammed also sees no demonstrable economic advantage for Kenya at this stage. Beyond security, factors such as tax administration, public services and governance also play a decisive role.

US Plans to Remove South Africa and Rwanda From AGOA in 2027, Putting $1.7 Billion in South African Preferential Exports at Risk
Ready
The United States plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA on 1 January 2027, citing trade barriers, governance concerns and national security interests. South Africa exported approximately $1.7 billion under AGOA in 2025, down from $4 billion in 2024, while Rwanda's total goods exports to the United States were $43.3 million and its apparel benefits have already been suspended since 2018. The decision comes as AGOA itself approaches its 31 December 2026 expiry date, creating uncertainty for African exporters and investors about both national eligibility and the future of the wider trade programme.
The United States has notified Congress of President Donald Trump's intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) effective 1 January 2027, threatening preferential market access for two African economies whose trade relationships with Washington differ substantially in size and structure. South Africa, the programme's largest beneficiary, exported approximately $1.7 billion in goods under AGOA in 2025, while Rwanda's total goods exports to the United States amounted to $43.3 million. The proposed exclusions follow Washington's annual eligibility review and arrive as Congress faces a separate decision over whether to renew AGOA itself, which is currently authorised only until 31 December 2026.
United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced the decision on 2 November, saying the administration had determined that both governments were engaging in practices inconsistent with AGOA eligibility requirements. Washington cited barriers to American trade and investment and concerns involving national security and foreign policy in both countries. It additionally identified corruption in South Africa and concerns about the rule of law, political pluralism, internationally recognised workers' rights and human rights in Rwanda. The announcement did not identify specific transactions or regulatory measures underlying each finding, leaving the two governments and affected businesses to assess how the decision might be reversed before its proposed effective date.
The immediate economic exposure is considerably larger in South Africa, where agricultural exporters, manufacturers and associated logistics businesses have developed commercial relationships around preferential access to the American market. Rwanda's bilateral goods trade is much smaller, and its apparel exports have been excluded from AGOA preferences since 2018. The political implications nevertheless extend beyond the direct value of preferential exports because the latest decision connects access to the American market with Washington's wider assessments of governance, investment conditions and foreign policy alignment.
South Africa's AGOA Exports Have Already Fallen From $4 Billion to $1.7 Billion
South Africa's Department of Trade, Industry and Competition reported that approximately $1.7 billion of the country's exports to the United States entered under AGOA in 2025, compared with $4 billion in 2024. That represents a decline of roughly 57.5 percent in the value of preferential exports over one year, before the proposed removal takes effect. The government's figures also show that AGOA exports accounted for approximately 10 percent of South African exports to the United States in 2025, down from 28 percent a year earlier, while around 89 percent of exports entered under ordinary World Trade Organization most favoured nation terms.
Those numbers establish an important distinction between the total bilateral trade relationship and the portion directly dependent on AGOA. South African exports to the United States would not automatically stop if the programme's benefits were withdrawn. Most already enter outside the preferential arrangement, and exporters could continue selling goods to American customers under the tariffs and rules applicable to their products. The commercial risk is concentrated in sectors where the loss of tariff preferences would increase landed costs enough to reduce margins, weaken competitiveness or make existing supply contracts less attractive.
The effects would vary considerably by product. Citrus exporters, wine producers and manufacturers supplying the American market may face different tariff rates, production costs and alternatives for redirecting goods. Agricultural exports are particularly sensitive to established buyer relationships, packaging specifications, seasonal shipping arrangements and distribution networks, while manufacturers may have invested in equipment and production systems designed around American customers. Even a relatively modest tariff increase can affect profitability where exporters operate on narrow margins and compete with suppliers from countries enjoying more favourable trade treatment.
The loss of AGOA preferences would also arrive after other American trade measures had already reduced the programme's commercial value. An August 2026 Congressional Research Service assessment noted that South African motor vehicles were subject to a separate 25 percent tariff under Section 232, while additional tariffs had been imposed on South Africa and certain other countries under Section 301. AGOA preferences do not automatically override these separate tariff measures, meaning some exporters have already been operating under a more restrictive trade environment despite their country's eligibility for the programme.
That distinction helps explain why the value of South African AGOA exports has fallen substantially without implying that every dollar of the decline resulted from a single policy decision. Changes in commodity prices, export volumes, product classifications, American demand and applicable tariffs can all affect the reported value of preferential trade.
South Africa's wider relationship with the United States remains economically substantial. Pretoria reported bilateral trade of $28.8 billion in 2025 and said more than 600 American companies operate in the country, supporting approximately 134,600 jobs. South Africa also supplies strategic mineral and industrial products to the American market, while some South African exporters purchase components and equipment from American manufacturers. The withdrawal of AGOA preferences would therefore affect particular commercial supply chains within a much larger relationship rather than terminate bilateral trade.
The South African government has disputed Washington's handling of the negotiations. Trade Minister Parks Tau said Pretoria had offered additional concessions beyond those agreed in 2015, while maintaining that the proposals respected South Africa's constitutional obligations, biosecurity requirements and World Trade Organization commitments. The government also argued that Washington had introduced new concerns that had not formed part of the discussions initiated in 2025.
Pretoria says it will continue engaging American authorities while supporting affected exporters and expanding market access elsewhere. Its diversification strategy identifies opportunities across the African Continental Free Trade Area, the European Union, the United Kingdom, India, China, Southeast Asia and Latin America. Redirecting existing exports, however, requires more than identifying new markets. Producers must establish commercial relationships, satisfy technical and regulatory requirements and compete against suppliers already serving those destinations.
Rwanda Faces a Smaller Trade Shock but a Wider Diplomatic Problem
Rwanda's exposure is different because its trade relationship with the United States is much smaller. The Office of the United States Trade Representative reports that American goods imports from Rwanda reached $43.3 million in 2025, an increase of 43.3 percent from the previous year, while American goods exports to Rwanda amounted to $39.1 million. Total bilateral goods trade was therefore $82.4 million, compared with $251 million in services trade.
The figures require careful interpretation. The $43.3 million represents total American merchandise imports from Rwanda, not the value of goods that actually received AGOA preferences. It would be inaccurate to present the entire amount as exports that will lose duty free status. Certain goods may already face zero ordinary tariffs, while others may enter under different customs arrangements. AGOA also applies to eligible merchandise rather than services, meaning the proposed removal does not directly withdraw the preferences governing Rwanda's considerably larger bilateral services relationship.
Rwanda has also faced restrictions under the programme before. In July 2018, the first Trump administration suspended Rwanda's AGOA apparel benefits following a dispute over tariffs and restrictions on imported secondhand clothing and footwear. Washington argued that Rwanda's measures restricted American trade, while Rwanda had been pursuing domestic textile and apparel development within a wider East African effort to reduce dependence on imported used clothing. The suspension affected apparel exports rather than removing Rwanda from the programme entirely, allowing other eligible products to continue receiving preferential treatment.
The 2026 announcement is therefore broader. It seeks to terminate Rwanda's country eligibility rather than suspend preferential treatment for one category of products. It also includes diplomatic and governance concerns beyond those that drove the earlier disagreement over secondhand clothing.
The timing is particularly consequential because the AGOA announcement followed additional American sanctions related to the conflict in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. articles.title: USD/ZAR Steady as US Plans to Remove South Africa From AGOA - EBC Financial Group
articles.summary: USD/ZAR Steady as US Plans to Remove South Africa From AGOA  EBC Financial Group
articles.full_text:
USD/ZAR was quoted near 16.61 on the evening of 3 November 2026, Eastern Standard Time (EST), after Washington announced plans to remove South Africa from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on 1 January 2027. The rand’s limited reaction contrasts with the potential cost to affected exporters.
Only about 10% of South Africa’s US-bound exports used AGOA preferences in 2025. Its loss would not stop bilateral trade, although agricultural exporters face concentrated risks.
South Africa also holds municipal elections on 4 November. The accompanying public holiday closes domestic central-bank trading and settlement, although international USD/ZAR dealing continues.
On 2 November, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer confirmed that President Donald Trump had notified Congress and the governments of South Africa and Rwanda of his intention to terminate their AGOA eligibility from 1 January 2027. The notification starts the required 60-day notice period; the change is not yet effective.
Washington cited barriers to American trade and investment, corruption, and concerns involving US national security and foreign policy. These are the administration’s stated reasons.
South African Trade Minister Parks Tau said Pretoria would continue engaging Washington while protecting affected industries. Pretoria argues that Washington raised new issues outside negotiations begun in 2025.
AGOA itself is not ending in January. US legislation signed on 2 September extended it through December 2028. The latest move concerns South Africa’s eligibility, not the wider programme’s existence. AGOA is a unilateral US trade preference, not a bilateral free-trade treaty; its advantages can be withdrawn following eligibility reviews.
USD/ZAR traded near 16.62 at 1:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time (EST) on 3 November, little changed from the previous close. By 8:04 a.m. EST, the pair had risen to approximately 16.6425, with the rand weakening around 0.3% on the day.
By the evening of 3 November EST, USD/ZAR had returned towards 16.61, suggesting that the planned AGOA withdrawal had yet to trigger sustained selling pressure on the South African currency.
ETM Analytics said the decision had largely been anticipated by markets. Business Unity South Africa similarly described Washington’s announcement as unsurprising given the state of bilateral relations. The limited initial price movement supports that interpretation, but cannot prove all future trade risks are priced in.
The currency also responds to the US dollar, international interest-rate expectations, commodity export receipts and imported energy costs. These forces can obscure the effect of a single trade announcement. The absence of a sharp decline in the rand is therefore consistent with a manageable direct tariff shock, but it cannot rule out a later increase in South Africa’s perceived political or investment risk.
South Africa’s trade ministry estimates that nearly $1.7 billion of exports to the US benefited from AGOA in 2025, down from about $4 billion in 2024. The preferential share of US-bound exports fell from about 28% to 10%. Around 89% already used ordinary most-favoured-nation terms in 2025.
AGOA shipments also represented approximately 1% of the country’s total global exports, according to the government. The national totals, however, conceal significant differences between export sectors.
| Measure | Verified Figure | What It Indicates | 
|---|---|---|
| AGOA-covered exports in 2025 | Nearly $1.7 billion | Trade using the preference, not exports that will disappear | 
| Share of US-bound exports under AGOA | Approximately 10% | Most trade was already outside the programme | 
| Estimated tariff savings in 2025 | Around $55 million | Direct value of the preference before withdrawal | 
| Average additional tariff on covered goods | About 3.6 percentage points | Estimated increase, not a tariff on all South African exports | 
Existing US national-security tariffs on South African vehicles, metals and other goods are estimated to impose around $450 million in annual duties. This substantially exceeds the approximately $55 million in tariff savings associated with AGOA in 2025, indicating that existing trade restrictions already carry a greater direct tariff burden than the preferences now at risk.
Neither figure forecasts lost sales or foreign-exchange earnings. US importers generally pay customs duties at the border, but the commercial burden can be shared if exporters reduce prices to retain customers. The effect on future dollar export receipts depends on volumes, not the announced tariff change alone.
Agriculture faces a particularly uneven impact. Citrus growers have invested in orchards designed for the US market, while plant-health rules and buyer preferences make diversion difficult. Some producers expect pressure on margins and employment once the preference ends.
Wine exporters also face reduced price competitiveness. Automotive producers have already been affected by separate US sector-specific tariffs, so losing AGOA would not create the same additional burden for every shipment. Actual tariff increases depend on each product and existing duties.
Potential job losses could reach several thousand, particularly among businesses dependent on exports to the US. However, these remain projections rather than confirmed employment losses. The impact on affected industries and local communities could therefore be more severe than the relatively modest effect on South Africa's overall economy.
South Africans vote in local government elections on Wednesday, 4 November. These polls select municipal representatives, not the national president or the South African Reserve Bank’s monetary-policy committee. Their direct currency impact is less certain than a national policy change.
Investors may nevertheless examine the results for evidence of municipal coalition stability and future delivery of infrastructure and basic services. Economic effects depend on eventual governance outcomes. Municipal service delivery and infrastructure reliability can affect investment costs, but local election results do not automatically reset national fiscal or monetary policy.
There is a more immediate market detail: the South African Reserve Bank has designated 4 November a non-trading and non-settlement day because of the public holiday. International currency dealing continues, although reduced local participation may affect liquidity and spreads.
Near-term price references include the 3 November trading range of approximately 16.53 to 16.68. Those are observed highs and lows, not independently validated support or resistance levels. Confirmation after domestic market activity resumes would be more informative than a brief holiday-session price excursion.
The next trade-policy catalyst is whether Washington and Pretoria produce a concrete change to the announced January eligibility decision. Until then, statements about possible compromise are not equivalent to a revised US decision. Exporters will monitor tariff classifications, buyers’ pricing decisions and alternative markets.
Beyond trade, the US October employment report is scheduled for 6 November, while South Africa’s next central-bank rate announcement is due on 19 November. Those releases could move USD/ZAR independently of AGOA. A stronger dollar or renewed energy-price pressure could weaken the rand; softer dollar conditions or better export receipts could work in the opposite direction.
USD/ZAR’s limited reaction to the AGOA announcement reflects a policy change with concentrated exporter exposure rather than an immediate halt to South African trade with America. South Africa’s benefits are set to end in January 2027, while the broader programme runs through 2028.
For USD/ZAR, the next decisive evidence will be changes to that policy, the commercial response of affected exporters and incoming US and South African economic data. The municipal election and local trading holiday warrant caution when interpreting any short-term currency moves.

articles.summary: COSATU blames AfriForum and Solidarity for US move to terminate South Africa’s AGOA access  https://weekendargus.co.za/
articles.full_text:
COSATU has accused AfriForum and Solidarity of helping fuel the diplomatic tensions behind the United States’ move to end South Africa’s participation in a major African trade programme, warning that workers and businesses could pay the price.
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) says lobbying by the two organisations has damaged South Africa’s relationship with Washington and contributed to the decision to terminate the country’s access to the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from January 1, 2027.
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to terminate South Africa’s participation in the programme, which provides eligible African countries with preferential access to the US market.
The announcement follows an annual review of sub-Saharan African countries’ eligibility for AGOA by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
Greer said Trump had determined that South Africa and Rwanda were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme’s eligibility requirements, including barriers to US trade and investment, as well as practices considered threats to US national security and foreign policy interests.
COSATU warns AGOA decision could put jobs at risk
COSATU said it was deeply concerned about the potential impact of South Africa’s removal from AGOA on agricultural and manufacturing jobs.
The programme has provided preferential access to the US market for South African exports and supported trade between African countries and the United States.
COSATU parliamentary co-ordinator Matthew Parks said the benefits extended beyond South Africa, including through regional supply chains.
He pointed to South African vehicle exports to the US that include components manufactured in neighbouring countries. AGOA had also benefited the US through the supply of African goods, including critical minerals, while helping create an estimated 200 000 direct jobs in the US, he said.
“The US, like all other nations, has the right to determine which goods can enter its market and at what tariff level. Other African countries have previously been removed from AGOA, and some were later reinstated,” Parks said.
However, he warned that South Africa’s exit could threaten thousands of jobs.
“We have already seen many jobs lost at factories and companies in Cape Town, Atlantis, Malmesbury and Tulbagh, amongst others. We have seen the devastation it threatens to these workers and farmers’ abilities to take care of their families,” he said.
COSATU has previously warned that racially divisive rhetoric could undermine South Africa’s AGOA trade benefits.
Government urged to negotiate with Washington
Parks called on the South African government to use the period before the proposed termination takes effect to negotiate an agreement that would protect the economy and jobs.
“Given South Africa’s already dangerously high 43.8% unemployment rate and weak economic growth, it is important that South Africa’s government utilise the next 60 days before this exit comes into effect, to negotiate a favourable set of solutions to avert this potential blow to the South African economy and jobs,” he said.
He said discussions should be based on facts and mutual respect, including recognition of South Africa as a constitutional democracy and a sovereign member of the international community.
Parks said negotiations over continued AGOA membership and efforts to reset bilateral relations with the US should prioritise South Africans’ interests and respect the country’s transformation journey.
He also called on the departments of Trade, Industry and Competition; Employment and Labour; National Treasury; and Agriculture to introduce urgent support measures for workers, businesses, industries and communities at risk.
“This must include subsidies and incentives, tax rebates and holidays, and support from the Unemployment Insurance Fund’s Temporary Employment Relief Scheme,” he said.
“We cannot afford to abandon a single worker, business, industry or community.”
Parks added that South Africa should accelerate efforts to diversify its export markets, including in Canada, Brazil, Europe, Asia and across the African continent, with support from government and the private sector.
COSATU says AfriForum and Solidarity must take responsibility
Parks also launched a sharp attack on AfriForum and Solidarity, accusing the organisations of contributing to strained relations between South Africa and the US through their lobbying efforts.
The two organisations have previously engaged with the Trump administration in Washington, including through a delegation that met representatives of the US president’s administration.
“It is long overdue that AfriForum, Solidarity and other proponents of the white persecution myths, appreciate the very real damage that their endless lobbying of and antics in the US have done to bilateral relations,” Parks said.
He argued that their efforts had contributed to South Africa’s removal from AGOA and said the consequences could be felt by workers and farmers across the country.
“They must now explain to white farmers from the vineyards of the Cape to the citrus farms in Limpopo; to White, Coloured, Indian and African workers from the clothing factories in Cape Town to the motor manufacturing plants in the Eastern Cape, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal why their livelihoods will now be lost.
“This is AfriForum, Solidarity et al’s legacy. They must own it,” he said.
Parks said COSATU would continue working with government and industry to ensure support measures were introduced. The federation would also engage with the US labour movement to protect workers’ jobs.
“South Africa is a resilient nation. It has overcome some of humanity's darkest moments. We will navigate these turbulent times too,” he said.
Tau says AGOA decision does not define broader US relationship
Meanwhile, Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said the US decision to move towards excluding South Africa from AGOA did not define the broader relationship between the two countries.
He warned, however, that finding a solution would depend on both sides’ willingness to engage.
Tau described the US as an important trade and investment partner and said South Africa remained committed to pursuing a mutually beneficial relationship.
“This decision does not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the United States, however a solution depends on the willingness of both Parties to find solutions,” he said.
He said the government would support affected sectors, protect South Africa’s national interests and continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the US.
“South Africa remains committed to a balanced and mutually beneficial partnership with the US that enables preferential trade that supports beneficiation of critical minerals at source and promotes investment,” he said.
Tau added that South Africa would continue to uphold its constitutional responsibilities, transformation objectives and international obligations while pursuing practical solutions to expand trade and investment.

articles.title: South Africa’s AGOA Crisis: What It Means for Zimbabwe’s Economy - The Zimbabwe Mail
articles.summary: South Africa’s AGOA Crisis: What It Means for Zimbabwe’s Economy  The Zimbabwe Mail
articles.full_text:
South Africa’s impending removal from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) is being treated largely as a diplomatic confrontation between Pretoria and Washington. For Zimbabwe, however, the implications are considerably wider. The decision exposes the vulnerability of an economy whose trade, manufacturing supply chains, fuel supplies, agricultural inputs and distribution networks remain deeply connected to its southern neighbour.
By Brighton Musonza
The immediate question is how South African exporters will absorb the loss of preferential access to the United States. The more important question for Zimbabwe is what happens when the largest economy in Southern Africa is forced to reorganise its trade relationships, redirect exports and reconsider the structure of its industrial supply chains.
Zimbabwe cannot afford to view this as somebody else’s trade dispute. Its economic relationship with South Africa is too substantial, too concentrated and too important to domestic production for the consequences to remain on the other side of the Limpopo.
Washington has notified Pretoria of its intention to remove South Africa from AGOA with effect from 1 January 2027. The programme, established in 2000, provides eligible sub-Saharan African countries with preferential access to the US market for thousands of products. South Africa became its largest beneficiary, building export industries around access to American consumers, particularly in automotive manufacturing, agriculture, food processing and selected industrial products.
The Southern African Agri Initiative estimates that 62,000 direct jobs could be at risk following the proposed withdrawal. Aluma Capital chief economist Frederick Mitchell has put the potential exposure considerably higher, estimating between 125,000 and 576,000 direct and indirect jobs. The wide range reflects different assumptions about the effects across supply chains, and should not be interpreted as a confirmed forecast of job losses.
The scale of the potential disruption is nevertheless significant. South Africa’s automotive industry, citrus and deciduous fruit producers, wine exporters and advanced manufacturing businesses have developed commercial relationships around the US market. Some agricultural producers have invested in orchards and production capacity specifically to serve American buyers. Redirecting those products to other destinations is not necessarily straightforward.
But the economic consequences will not stop at South Africa’s borders.
Zimbabwe’s exposure is much larger than the AGOA trade itself
Zimbabwe’s vulnerability begins with the structure of its external trade. South Africa is not simply a neighbouring country with which Zimbabwe exchanges goods. It is a major source of the machinery, fuel, food, chemicals, vehicles, plastics, steel and other industrial inputs that keep Zimbabwean businesses operating.
World Trade Organisation data, drawing on UN Comtrade, shows that South Africa supplied approximately 39.5% of Zimbabwe’s merchandise imports in 2024, equivalent to about US$3.77 billion. It also accounted for 27.6% of Zimbabwe’s exports, worth approximately US$2.05 billion.
Those figures reveal a relationship that is both commercially important and structurally imbalanced. Zimbabwe buys substantially more from South Africa than it sells there, leaving local businesses dependent on South African manufacturers, wholesalers and distribution networks for a considerable proportion of their requirements.
The composition of imports matters as much as the total value. Zimbabwe’s purchases from South Africa include cereals, machinery, mineral fuels, vehicles, plastics, iron and steel, electrical equipment and fertilisers. These are not merely consumer products that can be replaced without consequence. They are inputs into agriculture, mining, manufacturing, construction, transport and retail.
A disruption to South African production or distribution could therefore reach Zimbabwe through several channels. If manufacturers face higher costs, weaker export demand or reduced investment, those pressures may eventually be reflected in supplier prices, delivery times and the availability of industrial inputs.
This does not mean AGOA’s withdrawal will automatically make South African goods more expensive in Zimbabwe. The programme governs preferential access to the US market, not South African exports to Zimbabwe. The transmission would depend on how individual companies respond, whether they lose orders, how they reorganise production and whether the costs of adjusting their businesses are passed on to customers.
That distinction is important. Zimbabwe should prepare for possible spillovers without confusing a US trade preference decision with a direct tariff imposed on Zimbabwean imports.
The risk of a weaker South African industrial economy
The more immediate danger is that South African businesses exposed to the US market could experience weaker demand, lower margins and pressure to reduce operating costs.
The South African automotive sector illustrates the problem. Vehicle manufacturing is built around extensive supplier networks involving components, metals, plastics, logistics, engineering services and specialised labour. A reduction in export competitiveness can affect businesses well beyond the final vehicle assembly plants.
Zimbabwean companies supplying industrial materials, packaging, engineering services or other inputs into South African production networks could face indirect exposure where their customers are linked to affected export industries.
Agriculture presents another transmission channel. South Africa is a major regional producer and distributor of food. Its agricultural economy is connected to Zimbabwe through imports, wholesale markets, transport operators, packaging businesses and cross-border trade.
If South African fruit and agricultural exporters redirect products towards African markets after losing preferential access to the US, Zimbabwe could experience increased competition from imported produce. Local farmers and processors may face pressure in products where South African producers have advantages in scale, financing, technology and distribution.
This could be particularly challenging for Zimbabwean horticultural businesses seeking to expand commercial production. The country has ambitions to grow exports of citrus, avocados, blueberries, macadamia nuts and other high-value agricultural products. However, building a competitive export industry requires more than favourable growing conditions. It requires reliable logistics, cold-chain infrastructure, certification, access to finance and consistent market demand.
South Africa already possesses much of that commercial infrastructure. If its exporters intensify their search for regional customers, Zimbabwean producers will have to compete against companies with established supply chains and greater economies of scale.
The outcome could be a more competitive regional market, but not necessarily one in which Zimbabwean businesses automatically gain.
The opportunity hidden in South Africa’s trade difficulties
There is, however, another side to the argument. A restructuring of South African supply chains could create opportunities for Zimbabwean manufacturers and service providers capable of meeting the requirements of regional businesses.
South African companies may increasingly examine alternative sourcing arrangements, particularly where they can reduce costs, improve supply security or establish production partnerships elsewhere in the region.
Zimbabwe has an existing industrial base that could support some of this activity. Food processing, metal fabrication, packaging, chemicals, engineering, textiles, agricultural processing and mining-related manufacturing offer potential areas for deeper commercial cooperation.
The opportunity is not necessarily to replace South African manufacturers. It is to become a more useful part of their regional production networks.
For example, a Zimbabwean company producing packaging materials, industrial components or processed agricultural products could seek supply contracts with South African businesses. Mining companies operating across the region could also benefit from more integrated engineering, maintenance and equipment supply networks.
This is consistent with the direction of discussions at the South Africa–Zimbabwe Business Forum in August 2026. ZimTrade urged Zimbabwean companies to look beyond conventional exports and pursue opportunities in manufacturing, industrial supply chains, technology partnerships and regional distribution.
That is the correct strategic direction. Zimbabwe has spent too long treating exports largely as the movement of finished goods across borders rather than as an opportunity to participate in the production systems of larger regional economies.
However, investment will not follow political declarations. South African businesses will not relocate production or enter long-term supply agreements simply because Zimbabwe is geographically close. They will examine electricity reliability, currency and payment risks, taxation, labour productivity, infrastructure, border efficiency and the predictability of government policy.
Zimbabwe must compete on commercial terms.
The danger of becoming a dumping ground
One of the less discussed consequences of the AGOA decision is the possibility that South African exporters will redirect goods towards markets where they already have established commercial relationships.
Zimbabwe is an obvious destination because of its proximity, existing transport corridors and established distribution networks.
That could benefit consumers through greater product availability and competitive pricing. But it could also intensify pressure on domestic manufacturers already struggling with high production costs, expensive finance, unreliable electricity and competition from imports.

articles.title: After 26 years and five American presidents, what went wrong with South Africa's AGOA journey? - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: After 26 years and five American presidents, what went wrong with South Africa's AGOA journey?  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- South Africa will lose its preferential access to the US market under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA).
- AGOA, established in 2000, has provided duty-free access for African exporters to the US, supporting economic growth and market reforms across the continent.
- Since its inception, five US presidents have influenced AGOA’s terms, with legislative extensions, eligibility reviews, and suspensions tied to trade disputes, governance, and human rights concerns.
- South Africa's major AGOA dispute with the US emerged in 2015-2016 over agricultural import restrictions, resolved after negotiations and threatening of benefits suspension.
The announcement, however, has come with little surprise to trade observers, given the prolonged disagreements between the governments of both countries.
Since its establishment in 2000, AGOA has provided African exporters with preferential, duty-free access to the US market, the world’s largest economy, valued at approximately $33 trillion.
The Congressional Research Service (CRS), in its August 2026 report on the programme, explains that Congress designed AGOA to strengthen US-Africa trade and investment, promote economic growth through exports and encourage market-oriented reforms and respect for the rule of law.
Congress enacted the programme under the Trade and Development Act of 2000, which President Bill Clinton signed on May 18, 2000. South Africa became one of its leading beneficiaries, particularly in automotive manufacturing, agriculture, wine and other manufactured goods.
How five US presidents shaped AGOA
- Bill Clinton (2000): Establishment
Clinton signed the Trade and Development Act of 2000 on May 18, 2000, establishing AGOA. The programme offered eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential, duty-free access to the US market to promote exports, investment, industrialisation and economic growth.
- George W. Bush (2001–2009): Expansion
Congress expanded AGOA through amendments in 2002 and 2004, increasing market access and strengthening apparel provisions. The 2004 legislation extended the programme through September 30, 2015. In 2006, Congress extended the third-country fabric provision, allowing qualifying African garment manufacturers to source materials outside the continent while retaining duty-free benefits.
- Barack Obama (2009–2017): Renewal and stricter reviews
On June 29, 2015, Obama signed legislation extending AGOA through September 30, 2025. The renewal introduced out-of-cycle eligibility reviews, giving Washington greater flexibility to investigate beneficiary countries. His administration used this mechanism against South Africa over restrictions on US poultry, pork and beef imports, although the dispute was resolved in March 2016.
- Donald Trump (2017–2021): Eligibility enforcement
In 2018, Trump suspended Rwanda's duty-free treatment for apparel exports after the country maintained restrictions on imported secondhand clothing and footwear. Rwanda retained other AGOA benefits, but its apparel exports lost preferential treatment from July 31, 2018.
- Joe Biden (2021–2025): Continued enforcement
Biden maintained annual eligibility reviews. His administration terminated Ethiopia, Mali and Guinea from AGOA in 2022, followed by Gabon, Niger, Uganda and the Central African Republic in 2024, citing governance, human rights and rule-of-law concerns. The programme expired on September 30, 2025, without a new congressional extension.
- Donald Trump (2025–present): Reassessment and reciprocity
Trump signed legislation on February 3, 2026, retroactively reauthorising AGOA through December 31, 2026. His administration subsequently called for modernisation and greater trade reciprocity. It also announced its intention on November 2, 2026, to terminate South Africa and Rwanda's eligibility from January 1, 2027.
The first major clash: 2015–2016
South Africa’s first major AGOA dispute with Washington came in 2015, when the US challenged restrictions on American poultry, pork and beef exports.
On July 21, Washington launched an out-of-cycle eligibility review. In November, President Barack Obama threatened to suspend South Africa’s agricultural benefits unless Pretoria addressed the trade barriers, particularly restrictions on US bone-in chicken that had kept it out of the market for 15 years.
After negotiations, the first shipment of US frozen chicken legs arrived in Durban on February 26, 2016. South Africa also addressed outstanding requirements involving pork and beef. On March 14, Obama revoked the planned suspension, allowing the country to retain its agricultural benefits.
From trade disagreements to diplomatic tensions
Relations deteriorated during Donald Trump’s second presidency. At a May 2025 White House meeting, Trump raised allegations of discrimination against white South Africans and land seizures, which President Cyril Ramaphosa rejected.
Disputes over affirmative action, South Africa’s independent foreign policy and its genocide case against Israel further strained ties.
Despite the tensions, South Africa remained AGOA’s largest beneficiary by export value. However, its programme exports fell from about $4 billion in 2024 to $1.7 billion in 2025, according to figures reported by Reuters and cited by South African officials.
The 2025 figure represented roughly 10% of its exports to the US, while about 89% of US-bound exports entered under ordinary WTO terms.
Trump's 60-day notice and South Africa's response
In an October 28, 2026 letter, Trump gave South Africa 60 days' notice of his intention to terminate its AGOA eligibility from January 1, 2027. He cited alleged shortcomings in tackling corruption and trade barriers, alongside concerns over Pretoria's security relationships and foreign policy.
The US Trade Representative confirmed the decision on November 2. South Africa, meanwhile, said it would accelerate efforts to diversify export markets. Trade Minister Parks Tau told SABC News that the government would pursue opportunities across Africa, India, the EU and China to protect jobs.
The proposed termination would remove preferential tariff access for eligible South African goods, not end ordinary trade with the US.

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Bridge Expansion Bearings market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global bridge expansion bearings market is a critical segment of the civil engineering and construction sector, providing essential components that accommodate movement, rotation, and load transfer between bridge superstructures and substructures. These bearings are indispensable for structural integrity, safety, and longevity, enabling bridges to withstand thermal expansion, seismic activity, and dynamic traffic loads. The market's trajectory is closely tied to global infrastructure investment cycles, urbanization trends, and the pressing need to rehabilitate aging transport networks, particularly in developed economies.
From 2026 to 2035, the market is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 4.2%, reaching a market index of 152 (2025=100) by 2035. Growth is underpinned by sustained public and private investment in new transportation projects, especially in emerging Asia-Pacific economies, coupled with mandatory refurbishment programs in North America and Europe. Technological evolution toward advanced materials and smart bearing systems with integrated monitoring capabilities is creating new value segments. However, the market faces headwinds from cyclical construction downturns, volatile raw material costs, and project-driven procurement that leads to uneven order books.
The competitive landscape features a mix of large multinational engineering conglomerates and specialized mid-sized firms, with competition hinging on technical expertise, certification, and project delivery reliability. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of market dynamics, demand drivers, restraints, segmentation, and regional outlook to 2035.
The baseline scenario for the global bridge expansion bearings market anticipates steady growth from 2026 to 2035, with a CAGR of 4.2% and a market index reaching 152 by 2035 (2025=100). In mature markets like North America and Europe, the focus shifts toward rehabilitation and replacement of aging bridge stock, creating sustained demand for retrofit bearings, especially seismic isolation devices.
The highway bridge segment remains the largest end-use sector, supported by government stimulus packages and public-private partnerships. Railway bridge demand is expected to outpace other sectors due to high-speed rail and freight corridor projects. Technological advancements, including smart bearings with embedded sensors for real-time monitoring, are gaining traction, enabling predictive maintenance and extending service life. However, the market's project-based nature introduces volatility, with order books susceptible to delays and cancellations. Raw material price fluctuations, particularly for steel and rubber, pose margin pressures.
Geographically, Asia-Pacific will dominate consumption, while Latin America and the Middle East & Africa offer emerging opportunities amid infrastructure modernization. The competitive landscape is consolidating, with key players investing in R&D and geographic diversification to capture high-value projects. Overall, the market is poised for moderate but resilient growth, driven by the non-negotiable need for bridge safety and longevity.

- Increasing adoption of seismic isolation bearings in earthquake-prone regions, supported by stricter building codes.

- Technological advancements in smart bearings with integrated monitoring capabilities, enabling predictive maintenance.
- Urbanization and population growth in emerging economies, necessitating expansion of transportation networks.

- Complex and lengthy procurement processes for large infrastructure projects, resulting in extended sales cycles.

In developed markets, aging highway bridges require frequent bearing replacement and retrofit, creating a stable aftermarket. Demand-side indicators include government transportation budgets, highway construction starts, and average bridge age. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from increased infrastructure spending, especially in Asia-Pacific and North America, where many bridges are structurally deficient.
The shift toward longer-span bridges and higher traffic loads will necessitate advanced bearings with greater load capacity and durability. However, the segment's growth may be tempered by budget constraints and delays in public project funding. Current trend: Steady growth driven by new road infrastructure and rehabilitation projects..

Railway bearings must meet stringent performance standards to ensure safety and ride comfort, often requiring specialized designs such as spherical and pot bearings with enhanced fatigue resistance. New Delhi [India], November 4 (ANI): India has 1,782 identified export opportunity products across BRICS markets but accounts for only 8.4 per cent of the export share in the assessment, indicating significant untapped potential for Indian businesses to expand their presence within the grouping, according to a study by India Exim Bank and FICCI.
The study highlighted that India has the second-highest number of export opportunity products among BRICS members, after China. However, its relatively low export share highlights a gap between the country's export competitiveness and its presence in markets across the bloc.
'India on the other hand, presents a contrasting picture, where, despite having the second-highest number of identified products (1,782), it holds the lowest export share (8.4 per cent), suggesting considerable untapped potential relative to its competitiveness,' the report said.
The report identified pharmaceuticals, petroleum products, automobiles and components, and engineering goods as some of India's key export strengths in the Established-High-Potential category.
It said the opportunities for expanding trade among BRICS members were spread across several sectors, including manufacturing, technology, energy and industrial products.
The report also highlighted the broader trade potential of the 11-member grouping, which comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.
Collectively, BRICS economies generated a GDP of USD 31.6 trillion in 2024, accounting for 28.5 per cent of global output. Between 2015 and 2024, the grouping recorded a compound annual growth rate of 5.4 per cent.
In terms of trade, BRICS exports to the world stood at USD 7.2 trillion in 2024, while imports were estimated at USD 6.3 trillion.
However, merchandise exports among member countries accounted for 22.8 per cent of the bloc's total exports, indicating scope for deeper trade integration.
China remained the dominant economy in the grouping's export opportunity assessment, with 5,325 identified products and an export share of 48 per cent. Its opportunities in the Established-High-Potential and Emerging-High-Potential categories were valued at USD 333 billion.
The report said China's product opportunities were concentrated in electronics, telecommunications equipment, electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, solar modules and other renewable energy equipment.
It also identified opportunities for India and other BRICS economies in emerging products such as aerospace equipment, automotive components, specialised machinery, electrical equipment, medical products, chemicals and advanced engineering goods.
The study called for greater cooperation in manufacturing, technology development, research and innovation to help member countries build stronger cross-border supply chains.
It identified eight sectors with significant potential for cooperation, including critical minerals and energy storage, renewable energy equipment, green hydrogen, semiconductors and electronics, pharmaceuticals and medical devices, automobiles and electric vehicles, aerospace and advanced mobility, and smart manufacturing. South African unions urged the government Tuesday to work to save a US duty-free trade deal that supports thousands of jobs, while analysts played down the broader economic impact.
Washington announced Monday that from January 1 South Africa and Rwanda would be removed from the Africa-US trade preference programme granted to several countries.
About 10 percent of South African exports to the United States in 2025 entered under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) programme, which mainly covers the agriculture, manufacturing and automobile sectors.
The country's largest trade union federation, Cosatu, told AFP that between 3,000 and 10,000 agriculture and manufacturing jobs could be on the line.
Some of the companies most at risk are based in small towns, for example the citrus-producing areas of the Western Cape province, said Cosatu representative Matthew Parks.
"There's a danger of creating ghost towns," he said.
"We are meeting with government to encourage them to go to the US, use the next 60 days to negotiate a possible package deal," Parks said.
The Citrus Growers' Association of Southern Africa warned Monday that jobs and the economies of entire towns were at stake.
Strained diplomatic ties
South Africa is the largest beneficiary of AGOA, which grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the US market.
The deal has been renewed until the end of 2028 but South Africa and Rwanda were given notice of their removal after an annual review that cited "concerning" practices.
These include "barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests", a US statement said.
Pretoria had been prepared for exclusion because of its battered diplomatic ties with Washington over various domestic and international policy differences.
For the automobile sector, "the most severe blow" had been the Trump administration's 25-percent tariffs imposed in April 2025, said the Motor Industry Staff Association (MISA) union.
As a result, South African vehicle exports to the United States plunged by 83 percent to 4,136 units in 2025, it said in a statement.
"Government must make full use of the 60-day notice period because the possibility of reinstatement remains," it said, also calling for an "automotive trade solution".
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) programme was enacted in 2000. By GUILLEM SARTORIO (AFP/File)
"While the decision is significant and disappointing, it does not amount to a trade ban. South African vehicles will continue to be sold in the American market," MISA said.
International relations expert Kingsley Makhubela said it would be a "waste of time" for South Africa to appeal its removal.
"It's a political decision that has been made by the Trump administration; it's not a trade decision," he told AFP.
Makhubela said 134,000 jobs could be directly impacted, significant in an economy with an official unemployment rate running above 30 percent.
But Daryl Swanepoel, from the independent Inclusive Society Institute (ISI) policy research group, said claims of massive job losses were "alarmist" and assumed South African products would not be sold at all, which was not the case.
The United States will still need certain imports, for example citrus, even though they will be more expensive to consumers, he told AFP.
Minerals -- a major South African export -- remains exempted, he said, estimating the loss of AGOA would impact GDP by less than one percent.
"I believe the South African economy is mature enough to deal with this," Swanepoel said.
Removal from the duty-free deal "does not mean that all South African exports to the US will suddenly face new tariffs or disappear," said economist Johann Els, from PSG Financial Services.
While AGOA covered 10 percent of South African exports to the United States, this was just 0.7 percent of the country's total exports, he said in a statement.
"So, while the absolute numbers may look significant, the share of our overall exports directly affected is relatively small," he said.

articles.summary: Tanzania: African Development Bank, Tanzania close landmark $1.2 billion commercial financing for the Standard Gauge Railway  African Development Bank Group
articles.full_text:

Tanzania: African Development Bank, Tanzania close landmark $1.2 billion commercial financing for the Standard Gauge Railway
The United Republic of Tanzania has signed a $1.2 billion commercial financing facility for the Tabora–Kigoma section of its Standard Gauge Railway (Lot 6). The African Development Bank (AfDB), acting as Initial Mandated Lead Arranger (MLA), structured and arranged the Partial Credit Guarantee (PCG) of $800 million which is the Bank’s largest to date.
Tanzania mandated the Bank to structure and mobilise up to $3.2 billion for its regional railway development through Standard Gauge Railway Project. Delivering this ambitious project required a financing approach capable of mobilising capital from multiple investor classes. A key priority was to align the financing requirements and risk appetites of various institutions within a unified financing structure to support this strategic infrastructure investment, while managing the country’s other debts and various geopolitical political events which affected interest rates.
The operation combines the Bank’s transport sector expertise with its financial structuring and guarantee capabilities to advance the Central Corridor’s development as a productive regional economic corridor.
The Bank mobilised a nine-bank syndicate for the $1.2 billion commercial facility, co-arranged by Deutsche Bank and Société Générale. Other lenders include HSBC, Commerzbank, Nedbank, Stanbic Bank Tanzania, First Abu Dhabi Bank, FirstBank UK and Bank of Africa United Kingdom. Their commitments comprise $720 million of guaranteed lending and $480 million of lending based on clean risk to the sovereign. The $1.2 billion signed facility forms part of the overall $2.3 billion financing package, which outside of this commercial tranche comprises an ECA tranche and a further tranche to be mobilised in collaboration with a co-guarantor, all within the Bank’s broader mobilisation mandate.
The transaction illustrates blended finance in practice. At the centre of the commercial tranche is a non-market priced AfDB PCG of up to $800 million, covering the principal of the covered tranche plus two years of interest. AfDB remains Guarantor of Record, while credit insurance arranged by insurance broker Texel distributes $405.5 million of exposure to a panel of international insurers, including Lloyd’s syndicates. This brings additional private sector risk-bearing capacity into the transaction, strengthening the guarantee structure and enabling greater commercial financing to be mobilised for Tanzania’s railway development.
The financing will support the construction of the 411-kilometre electrified Tabora–Kigoma line, known as Lot 6, a strategic link in Tanzania’s railway network. For Tanzania, the investment will support the development of western regions by providing a long-haul high-volume transport link for production and trade. Farmers, mining operators and the general population are expected to benefit from more efficient transport, lower transport costs and employment opportunities during construction and operation. Connected to Tanzania’s wider railway network and the port of Dar es Salaam, the line will also support trade with the Democratic Republic of Congo across Lake Tanganyika through Kigoma and Kalemie ports, while the wider regional railway programme will strengthen links with Burundi and further into Eastern DRC.
“By combining development finance, commercial lending and insurance capacity, we have successfully unlocked the scale of financing required to deliver this type of transformational regional infrastructure. It reflects the vision behind the New African Financial Architecture for Development (NAFAD), focusing on private capital mobilization and partnerships in risk sharing to mobilise resources at scale,” said Max Ndiaye, Senior Director African Development Bank Group.
“The strategic value of this railway lies in the productive investment it can unlock along the Central Corridor. By connecting agricultural and mineral production areas, industrial centres and markets, the investment can strengthen regional value chains and expand opportunities for businesses and communities. Our ambition is to translate this landmark financing into a corridor that supports competitive industries, creates jobs and deepens regional integration,” said Mike Salawou, Director of the African Development Bank’s Infrastructure and Urban Development Department.
The transaction advances the Bank Group’s Ten-Year Strategy 2024–2033 and its Four Cardinal Points, particularly unlocking Africa’s capital and building resilient infrastructure and competitive value chains. By mobilising commercial finance for a regional transport corridor, it translates the Bank’s capital mobilisation mandate into tangible support for trade, industrial development and regional integration. It also illustrates how the Bank leverages its infrastructure expertise and financing capabilities to strengthen regional competitiveness and generate sustainable economic opportunities.
