articles.title: Kenya ports expand capacity amid growing interests by global shipping lines - The Star, Kenya
articles.summary: Kenya ports expand capacity amid growing interests by global shipping lines  The Star, Kenya
articles.full_text:
KENYA is expanding its port infrastructure and eliminating trade bottlenecks as global shipping lines increase interest in the country's maritime network.
This comes at a time when there is growing competition from Tanzania for regional cargo.
The Kenya Ports Authority is advancing expansion projects at the Port of Mombasa to accommodate larger vessels and rising cargo volumes.
The latest global shipping lines, to show interest in Kenya is Taiwan's Evergreen Line which has renewed attention on the commercial opportunities emerging along the East African coast.
The world's seventh-largest container shipping line is investing in a new generation of vessels, including ultra-large ships capable of carrying 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), with Mombasa among its major destinations in the Indian Ocean.
Last week, French shipping giant CMA CGM took the cargo battle inland with a dedicated rail freight service linking Kilindini harbour to Nairobi’s Embakasi Inland Container Depot (ICD)
Evergreen President K.H. Wu, accompanied by a company delegation and Bahaa Badr, chairman of Gulf Badr, the shipping line's agent, visited Mombasa this week for discussions on port infrastructure, operational capacity and the outlook for maritime trade.
The shipping line has ordered 23 feeder and medium-sized container ships and 11 liquefied natural gas (LNG) dual-fuel mega vessels, reflecting its strategy to expand regional cargo distribution and long-haul shipping.
Representing KPA chief executive William Ruto, General Manager Cargo Operations Sudi Mwasinago outlined the authority's expansion programme, including the imminent completion of Berth 19B.
The facility is expected to add approximately 300,000 TEUs (containers) to Mombasa's annual container handling capacity, while planned developments at Berths 23 and 24 will further increase the port's ability to handle growing cargo volumes.
“Mombasa remains the main maritime gateway for Kenya and the Northern Corridor, while the Port of Lamu offers additional capacity and a longer-term platform for regional trade, mainly transshipment,” Sudi noted.
KPA projects that combined annual cargo volumes across its ports will reach 168 million metric tonnes by 2045, compared with 45.45 million tonnes handled at Mombasa in 2025.
The projections underscore the importance of infrastructure investment as Kenya seeks to strengthen its position as a gateway for landlocked East and Central African economies.
Evergreen operates approximately 244 container ships with a combined capacity of 2.06 million TEUs, representing about 5.9 per cent of global container shipping capacity.
Top 10 container shipping lines (global ranking) are MSC (Mediterranean Shipping Company) (Switzerland) which has a 21.5 per cent share of global cargo, Maersk (Denmark) 13.5 per cent, CMA CGM Group (France) 12.9 per cent, COSCO Group (China) 10.6 per cent and Hapag-Lloyd (Germany) 6.9 per cent.
Others are ONE (Ocean Network Express) (Japan) with a 6.4 per cent share, Evergreen Line (Taiwan) 5.9 per cent, HMM Co Ltd (South Korea) three percent, Yang Ming Marine Transport Corp. (Taiwan) 2.2 per cent and Zim (Israel) with a two per cent share.
The infrastructure push comes as Kenya faces growing pressure to improve the efficiency of its trade corridors, with Tanzania increasingly attracting cargo through the Port of Dar es Salaam.
A recent report by the State Department for East African Community Affairs indicated Kenya was losing between five and eight per cent of high-value transit cargo annually, partly due to inefficiencies and non-tariff barriers along the Northern Corridor.
The 1,700-kilometre corridor, linking Mombasa to Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan and eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, handles more than 35.84 million metric tonnes of cargo annually and accounts for over 80 per cent of Kenya's transit trade.
It remains the region's main trade corridor with Tanzania (Dar es Salaam) serving the region through the 1,300 kilometre-long corridor.
A recent monitoring exercise found that persistent bottlenecks were undermining tye Northern Corridor's competitiveness, which Kenya has since moved to address, including reducing the number of roadblocks on the roads and speeding up cargo clearence.
According to EAC Affairs Principal Secretary Caroline Karugu said, the government has committed to reducing roadblocks to fewer than five gazetted stops, cutting Regional Electronic Cargo Tracking System response times from four to six hours to less than one hour, and restoring transit times to between 36 and 48 hours.
Reducing delays by half is estimated to save transporters between $288 (Sh37,172) and $360 (Sh46,465) per trip, while eliminating delay-related barriers could generate annual national savings of between $43 million (Sh5.6 billion) and $54 million (Sh6.9 billion).

articles.title: Africa can raise intra-African trade to 30% with reforms – AfCFTA - CitiNewsroom.com
articles.summary: Africa can raise intra-African trade to 30% with reforms – AfCFTA  CitiNewsroom.com
articles.full_text:
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat has indicated that Africa can increase trade among its member states to at least 30% if governments implement the necessary regulatory and infrastructure reforms.
Intra-African trade currently accounts for between 14% and 18%, falling short of the African Union’s target of 30%.
Speaking on the Citi Breakfast Show on Wednesday, November 4, Dr. Makong Tsotetsi, Director of Coordination and Programmes at the AfCFTA Secretariat said the continent must deepen its economic integration by removing barriers that make it difficult for businesses to trade across national borders.
Dr. Tsotetsi identified stringent regulations and difficulties in meeting product standards as some of the challenges restricting the movement of goods within the continent.
He said women and young people, in particular, face difficulties crossing borders to conduct business, a situation he believes must be addressed if Africa is to achieve its trade ambitions.
“At least, we should be at 30% now. But getting to that 30%, it takes a lot in terms of the reforms that the member states would have to undertake. If regulations are stringent, it is difficult for our women and youth to cross our borders,” he said.
He further stressed the need for member states to strengthen product quality standards to ensure that goods traded across borders meet the required safety requirements and do not pose health risks to consumers.
Beyond regulatory changes, Dr. Tsotetsi called for investment in relevant infrastructure to support the efficient movement of goods between African countries.
He maintained that achieving the 30% target would require governments to move beyond commitments and undertake practical reforms that make cross-border trade easier and more accessible.
Dr. Tsotetsi said addressing these challenges would be critical to unlocking the benefits of the AfCFTA and strengthening economic integration across the continent.

articles.title: AGOA Exclusion: SA Faces Economic Bow as US Withdraws Trade Privileges - African Times
articles.summary: AGOA Exclusion: SA Faces Economic Bow as US Withdraws Trade Privileges  African Times
articles.full_text:
South African workers in the automotive, agricultural and manufacturing sectors could face an uncertain future after the United States announced plans to withdraw the country’s preferential trade benefits, threatening businesses that rely on access to the American market.
The US government has given South Africa 60 days’ notice of its intention to remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), with the withdrawal expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
The decision has raised concerns about the future of South African exports, particularly vehicles, agricultural produce and manufactured goods, with the government acknowledging that workers, businesses and communities linked to industries benefiting from the agreement could be affected.
AGOA, introduced in 2000, allows eligible African countries to export certain goods to the US without paying import duties, making their products more competitive in one of the world’s largest consumer markets.
For South Africa, losing these benefits could make some exports more expensive for American buyers, potentially affecting demand and putting pressure on companies that depend on the trade relationship.
The Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (the dtic) said government was working with affected industries to assess the implications of the US decision and determine what support could be provided.
It said the impact would differ across sectors and that assistance would be considered on a company-by-company basis.
Government also plans to engage social partners to strengthen support for productive industries, protect jobs and help businesses find alternative export markets.
Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said the decision did not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the US.
He said finding a solution would depend on both countries being willing to engage constructively.
“At the same time, government will support affected sectors, protect South Africa’s national interests and continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the United States,” Tau said.
Government said it had made efforts to address concerns raised by Washington during negotiations that began in 2025.
According to the department, South Africa had offered additional concessions beyond those agreed to in 2015 through the appropriate channels.
However, it said the US had subsequently raised new issues that had not formed part of the earlier negotiations.
Despite the looming withdrawal, the government stressed that AGOA was not the foundation of the entire trade relationship between the two countries.
In 2025, South African exports to the US under AGOA were worth approximately US$1.7 billion, down from US$4 billion in 2024.
AGOA-related exports accounted for about 10% of South Africa’s exports to the US in 2025, compared with 28% the previous year, and represented approximately 1% of the country’s total exports worldwide.
The department said about 89% of South African exports to the US in 2025 entered under ordinary World Trade Organisation trade terms rather than AGOA preferences.
Bilateral trade between the two countries reached US$28.8 billion in 2025, while more than 600 American companies operating in South Africa support approximately 134,600 jobs.
South Africa also supplies 12 of the 50 minerals regarded as critical by the US and provides about 70% of the isotopes used by the country, including in cancer treatment.
The government warned that losing AGOA benefits could also disrupt existing business relationships and investments between the two countries.
It said South African manufacturers in industries such as vehicle production and boat building also rely on American inputs to manufacture goods for export.
The Democratic Alliance (DA), however, blamed the government’s handling of diplomatic relations with Washington for the looming exclusion.
DA spokesperson on International Relations and Cooperation Ryan Smith said South Africa’s removal from AGOA was avoidable and accused International Relations Minister Ronald Lamola of failing to protect the country’s economic interests.
Smith said the decision was a serious blow to agriculture, agro-processing, automotive manufacturing and mining, warning that workers employed in industries dependent on access to the American market could bear the consequences.
He accused the ANC government of allowing ideological differences and its approach to international relations to undermine trade negotiations with one of South Africa’s major trading partners.
The DA also argued that the government had failed to respond adequately to concerns raised by the administration of US President Donald Trump.
Smith said a DA-led national government would prioritise restoring preferential access to the American market and expanding South Africa’s international trade opportunities.
Meanwhile, the government said it would accelerate efforts to diversify export markets rather than rely heavily on one trading partner.
Potential opportunities include the African Continental Free Trade Area, the Southern African Development Community, India, China, the European Union, the United Kingdom and markets in South America and Southeast Asia.
The department also pointed to new export opportunities for South African citrus, avocados, grapes and apples.
Government maintained that South Africa remained committed to a mutually beneficial relationship with the US while protecting its constitutional obligations and national interests.
For businesses and workers whose livelihoods are connected to exports, however, the coming months will be critical as the government attempts to prevent the trade dispute from turning into a deeper economic setback.

articles.title: DINKO BOIKANYO | SA removal from Agoa: Which US orders can we keep and where do we sell next? - Sowetan
articles.summary: DINKO BOIKANYO | SA removal from Agoa: Which US orders can we keep and where do we sell next?  Sowetan
articles.full_text:
A citrus exporter in the Western Cape quoting an American buyer for next season has a decision to make.
If the fruit enters the US after January 1 2027 and the tariff preference falls away, who carries the extra cost?
The importer could accept a lower margin, ask the exporter to reduce its price or turn to another supplier.
The answer may determine how much fruit the grower can sell and how many shifts the packhouse can run. That is how a trade decision in Washington becomes an employment decision in South Africa.
On November 2, Washington announced that President Donald Trump had notified Congress and the governments of South Africa and Rwanda of his intention to terminate their eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) from January 1.
The programme itself has been extended through December 2028. The distinction matters because eligible competitors can retain preferences that South African suppliers stand to lose.
Pretoria has described the 60 days as an advance notice period and says it remains engaged with Washington. Exporters have to make commercial decisions while those discussions continue.
Modest national exposure can mask serious local shock
Introduced in 2000, Agoa offered qualifying goods from eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US without requiring equivalent tariff preferences in return. Its value went beyond the saving on an individual shipment.
It helped South African producers make the case for investing in certification, specialised equipment and buyer relationships. The programme’s lapse in September 2025 and retroactive renewal in February 2026 exposed a tension that the latest announcement brings into focus.
A factory or packhouse is built to serve customers for years, while the policy supporting its business case can change between one order and the next.
South African government figures put exports under Agoa at about US$4bn (about R662bn) in 2024 and US$1.7bn in 2025. In 2025, they represented around 10% of South African exports to the US and about 1% of the country’s total exports worldwide.
These figures describe the value of trade using the preference. The eventual loss of sales will depend on tariff rates, the availability of competing suppliers and how buyers respond.
The burden will also be uneven. Passenger vehicles and parts accounted for nearly two-thirds of South Africa’s Agoa-eligible products in 2024, according to the US Congressional Research Service. Vehicles already face separate US tariffs, so the incremental effect of losing Agoa has to be established at the product level.
The greater risk lies in the concentration of that exposure. An order that barely registers in national trade statistics can keep a production line running or carry a packhouse through part of its season.
A small component maker may lose work even though it has never been exported directly. The global value chain perspective helps explain why. The importer pays the duty at the border, but the cost moves through the supply chain according to who can switch suppliers, find another customer or afford to wait.
A retailer with several approved sources can push for a discount. A manufacturer that would need months to qualify a substitute has more reason to share the cost.
Defend the US orders that still make commercial sense
Every exposed exporter should review its largest orders with its US importer and customs broker. For each product, establish whether it currently claims Agoa, what ordinary US duty would apply if the preference ends, and how any separate tariffs or exemptions affect the calculation.
Check when the goods are expected to enter US customs and who bears the duty under the contract. A shipment leaving Durban in December may enter the US in January. That exercise should lead directly to a conversation with the buyer.
For a citrus producer, the negotiating case may rest on reliability during a particular supply window. For a vehicle component maker or a specialist boatbuilder, it may rest on the buyer’s cost of qualifying another supplier or arranging comparable after-sales support.
Where the relationship warrants a price concession, the exporter should ask for something of commercial value in return, such as a minimum volume commitment or a temporary adjustment with a review date.
The relevant test is whether the order still contributes enough after duty, freight, financing and the cost of serving the customer.
Cost reduction and product upgrading belong in the same calculation. Better cold-chain planning can cut spoilage. Coordinating delivery and production schedules can reduce storage costs or emergency freight.
Processing fruit locally may create a higher-value export or a use for fruit outside fresh-market specifications, provided there is a buyer and the finished product’s tariff, processing costs and achievable price support the investment.
Domestic value addition earns its place in the strategy when it improves the economics of the order.
Diversify through customers, not just countries
The revised Uppsala model of internationalisation, developed by Jan Johanson and Jan-Erik Vahlne, explains why exporters struggle when they sit outside the business networks that matter in a foreign market.
A distributor can provide knowledge that a market report rarely captures, including who buys, which specifications are negotiable and how reliably customers pay.
Firms can use that knowledge to test demand in stages. Start with a credible local partner and a trial shipment. Commit more stock or capital once a repeat order demonstrates that the relationship can work.
Africa offers a practical place to apply that approach. South Africa began preferential trading under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) in January 2024, with initial manufactured shipments to Ghana and Kenya.
In Southern Africa, existing Sadc preferences remain relevant where applicable. The commercial opportunity includes building regional supply and service networks. A South African equipment manufacturer entering Kenya, for example, could partner with a local firm that stocks parts and services machines.
For the customer, the ability to get a machine running again may be decisive. For the exporter, the partnership creates a reason for the customer to buy again. Firms should assess rules of origin, border times and payment risk alongside the tariff preference.
Brics can help build commercial relationships, with access terms determined market by market. China’s temporary zero-duty scheme for qualifying South African goods runs from May 2026 to April 2028, subject to the applicable tariff schedule and rules of origin.
An exporter considering China still needs to establish whether the product has the necessary approvals, which buyers will take it and what margin remains after freight and distribution. The same discipline applies to India, Canada, the EU, the UK and the Gulf.
The gravity model of trade explains why market size is only part of the opportunity. Trade depends on the cost of reaching a market relative to the alternatives. For a grower, a longer voyage can consume a tariff saving through freight and spoilage.
For an industrial exporter, an established service partner can make a smaller market more attractive than a larger one.
Give trade diplomacy a commercial brief
Washington cited barriers to US trade and investment, corruption, and national security and foreign policy concerns. Pretoria says it has offered concessions and that Washington has raised issues outside the scope of talks already under way.
The immediate task is to seek specific, written concerns and separate questions that officials can address through technical negotiations from those that require higher-level diplomacy.
Where agricultural market access is at issue, for example, officials should distinguish tariff or quota questions from animal-health safeguards.
Pretoria should press for continued eligibility and explore transitional or sector-specific relief where feasible. American importers and distributors can add weight to that effort by documenting the cost of changing suppliers and the consequences for their own customers and workers.
At home, the department of trade, industry and competition should use chambers, industry associations and organised labour to identify where exposure is concentrated.
Exporters with viable orders may need quick access to customs advice or working capital. Firms with a credible buyer in a new market may need help with certification or an unresolved market-access barrier. Smaller suppliers may need to be identified through the exporters they serve.
This work should inform the broader competitiveness agenda. A less costly port delay, a more reliable rail service or fewer interruptions to production can improve margins on every route a firm serves.
By January, a citrus exporter should know which American orders it can keep, how much of the extra duty it can afford to absorb and which new buyer is ready to take a trial shipment.
Pretoria, for its part, should be able to show Washington what those orders sustain on both sides of the Atlantic, from packhouse shifts and suppliers in South Africa to the American importers and distributors that rely on them.
Keeping an American order can help keep the packhouse running this season. When a new customer comes back for a second shipment, the grower has another buyer to count on when planning the next crop.
- Prof Boikanyo is an academic at the University of Johannesburg. He writes in his own personal capacity

articles.title: AGOA exclusion unlikely to have major impact on SA economy – economist - Jacaranda FM
articles.summary: AGOA exclusion unlikely to have major impact on SA economy – economist  Jacaranda FM
articles.full_text:
Independent economist Duma Gqubule says South Africa's exclusion from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) is unlikely to have a significant impact on the country's economy, arguing that the consequences have been overstated.
Gqubule says only about 10 % of South Africa's exports to the United States are affected by the loss of preferential trade access, amounting to approximately R14.8 billion.
He estimates that the loss of the tariff advantage could translate into a competitive disadvantage of about R500 million, which he believes is relatively small in the context of the broader economy.
The economist says South Africans should not be overly concerned about the decision, adding that exporters are unlikely to lose the American market entirely.
"I think South Africans must not be hysterical about the impact of AGOA; our exports in 2025 to the United States were R148 billion. The affected AGOA exports are 10% of total exports to the US, so that is R14.8 billion."
READ: Govt ‘to assess’ impact of AGOA exclusion
He argues that American consumers who prefer South African products, including oranges and locally manufactured vehicles, may continue buying them despite the additional tariffs.
Gqubule says the broader tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump on trading partners could have a greater impact on South African exports than the loss of AGOA preferences.
He also believes the strengthening of the rand presents a bigger challenge to local exporters.
"The exchange rate has appreciated recently, and that's going to have much more negative impact on exports than AGOA. So our rand is strong, and a good rand is not good for exports."
Gqubule argues that South Africa should consider a weaker currency as part of a broader strategy to improve export competitiveness, pointing to Japan, China and other Asian economies that have used similar approaches to expand their global market share.
He says the country should also use the current trade developments as an opportunity to strengthen its industrial policy and diversify its export markets.
Gqubule estimates that South Africa currently spends about 0.3 to 0.4% of its GDP on industrial policy, including incentives provided to businesses through the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition and the Industrial Development Corporation.
He believes this level of support is inadequate to help local companies compete internationally and access alternative markets.
"If you want to industrialise our country, we have to have much stronger support from the National Treasury to be able to provide direct support for our exporters to conquer world markets and diversify."
Citing China's investment in its electric vehicle industry, Gqubule says substantial government incentives can help local industries develop new products and become competitive global players.
He says South Africa should focus on adding value to its agricultural and mineral products instead of relying heavily on the export of raw materials.
More than half of the country's export basket consists of unbeneficiated mineral exports, according to Gqubule.
"We have to diversify our export basket irrespective of AGOA. We need to diversify from the excessive dependence on mineral exports and unbeneficiated mineral exports."
He adds that South Africa needs to expand manufacturing and services exports while developing stronger trade relationships beyond traditional markets.
On the diplomatic tensions between Pretoria and Washington, Gqubule says he does not believe the AGOA exclusion should fundamentally change South Africa's broader relationship with the United States.
He also questioned some of Washington's criticisms of South Africa's black economic empowerment policies, arguing that several American companies operating locally have participated in empowerment initiatives.
Gqubule says South Africa should remain focused on strengthening its productive capacity, supporting exporters and expanding its international trade opportunities rather than viewing the loss of AGOA preferences as an economic catastrophe.

The Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) has blamed lobby groups AfriForum and Solidarity for contributing to strained relations between South Africa and the United States, blaming their lobbying efforts for playing a role in Washington’s move to remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA).
This follows US President Donald Trump’s notification to Congress of his intention to terminate South Africa’s participation in the trade programme from January 1, 2027.
The announcement, made on Monday, represents a major setback for Pretoria’s efforts to retain preferential access to the US market amid growing tensions between the two countries.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the decision followed an annual review of sub-Saharan African countries’ eligibility for AGOA.
Greer said Trump had determined that South Africa and Rwanda were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme’s eligibility requirements, including barriers to US trade and investment, as well as practices considered threats to US national security and foreign policy interests.
COSATU warns of job losses
COSATU said it had noted the US government’s decision to remove South Africa from AGOA, which provides eligible African countries with preferential access to the US market.
“AGOA has provided lower tariff access to various African exports to the US market, currently the world’s largest economy. It has played an important role in boosting South African and many other African countries’ exports to the US,” said Cosatu parliamentary co-ordinator Matthew Parks.
Parks said the programme had also helped nurture intra-African trade, pointing to South African vehicle exports to the US that include components manufactured in neighbouring countries.
He added that AGOA had benefited the US through the supply of African goods, including critical minerals, while helping to create an estimated 200,000 direct jobs in the US.
“The US, like all other nations, has the right to determine which goods can enter its market and at what tariff level. Other African countries have previously been removed from AGOA, and some were later reinstated,” he said.
However, Parks said COSATU was deeply concerned about the impact South Africa’s exit from AGOA would have on thousands of agricultural and manufacturing jobs.
“We have already seen many jobs lost at factories and companies in Cape Town, Atlantis, Malmesbury and Tulbagh, amongst others. We have seen the devastation it threatens to these workers and farmers’ abilities to take care of their families,” he said.
Government urged to negotiate with US
Parks called on the South African government to use the period before the proposed termination takes effect to negotiate solutions that would protect the country’s economy and jobs.
“Given South Africa’s already dangerously high 43.8% unemployment rate and weak economic growth, it is important that South Africa’s government utilise the next 60 days before this exit comes into effect, to negotiate a favourable set of solutions to avert this potential blow to the South African economy and jobs,” he said.
He said the engagements should be based on facts and mutual respect, including recognition of South Africa as a constitutional democracy and a sovereign member of the international community.
Parks said negotiations over South Africa’s continued membership of AGOA and efforts to reset bilateral relations with the US should prioritise the interests of South Africans and respect the country’s transformation journey.
He also called on the departments of Trade, Industry and Competition; Employment and Labour; National Treasury; and Agriculture to urgently introduce support measures for workers, businesses, industries and communities at risk.
“This must include subsidies and incentives, tax rebates and holidays, and support from the Unemployment Insurance Fund’s Temporary Employment Relief Scheme,” he said.
“We cannot afford to abandon a single worker, business, industry or community.”
Parks added that efforts to diversify South Africa’s export markets, including in Canada, Brazil, Europe, Asia and across the African continent, should be accelerated with support from government and the private sector.
COSATU criticises AfriForum and Solidarity
Parks also criticised lobby groups AfriForum and Solidarity, accusing them of contributing to strained relations between South Africa and the US through their lobbying efforts.
“It is long overdue that AfriForum, Solidarity and other proponents of the white persecution myths, appreciate the very real damage that their endless lobbying of and antics in the US have done to bilateral relations,” he said.
He argued that South Africa’s removal from AGOA was, in part, a result of their efforts to undermine the country’s international standing.
“They must now explain to white farmers from the vineyards of the Cape to the citrus farms in Limpopo; to White, Coloured, Indian and African workers from the clothing factories in Cape Town to the motor manufacturing plants in the Eastern Cape, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal why their livelihoods will now be lost.
“This is AfriForum, Solidarity et al’s legacy. They must own it,” he said.
Parks said COSATU would continue working with government and industry to ensure support measures were introduced. The federation would also engage with the US labour movement to protect workers’ jobs.
“South Africa is a resilient nation. It has overcome some of humanity's darkest moments. We will navigate these turbulent times too,” he said.
Tau says AGOA decision does not define broader relationship
However, he warned that finding a solution would depend on both parties’ willingness to engage.
Tau described the US as an important trade and investment partner and said South Africa remained committed to pursuing a mutually beneficial relationship.
“This decision does not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the United States, however a solution depends on the willingness of both Parties to find solutions,” he said.
He said the government would support affected sectors, protect South Africa’s national interests and continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the US.
“South Africa remains committed to a balanced and mutually beneficial partnership with the US that enables preferential trade that supports beneficiation of critical minerals at source and promotes investment,” he said.
Tau added that South Africa would continue to uphold its constitutional responsibilities, transformation objectives and international obligations while pursuing practical solutions to expand trade and investment.

articles.title: CLARENCE TSHITEREKE | SA set to accelerate transition to Asia after Agoa exit - Business Day
articles.summary: CLARENCE TSHITEREKE | SA set to accelerate transition to Asia after Agoa exit  Business Day
articles.full_text:
The US decision to terminate South Africa’s eligibility under the African Growth & Opportunity Act (Agoa) from January next year marks a major shift in external economic relations. Citing trade barriers, corruption and foreign policy concerns, Washington is ending more than two decades of preferential access for South African exporters.
Agoa has underpinned South Africa’s trade with the US since 2000, providing duty-free access for more than 1,800 products, including vehicles, agricultural products, wine, steel and manufactured goods. South Africa has been among its largest beneficiaries. Exclusion raises questions beyond immediate export losses: how should South Africa position its economy in a multipolar world?
Adjustment costs may accelerate the transition towards Asia, critical minerals and value-added beneficiation. The immediate impact will be uneven: higher tariffs on automotive manufacturing and components, citrus, wine, macadamia nuts and other agricultural exports threaten their competitiveness, local investment and employment in affected industries and regions.
The shock nevertheless requires perspective. The political importance of the programme has often exceeded its direct macroeconomic contribution. South Africa accounted for about $3.76bn of the $8bn in Agoa imports entering the US in 2024.
Following Stats SA’s rebasing exercise last month, the country’s GDP is now estimated at R8-trillion, some $486bn at the current exchange rate, meaning Agoa-supported exports amount to less than 1% of that economic base. That is important but insufficient to determine the economy’s trajectory.
This comparison offers perspective, not grounds for complacency. A small share of national output can still represent substantial exposure for specific exporters that are dependent on preferential access. Policy should therefore carefully distinguish the economy’s capacity to absorb the shock from adjustment pressures facing individual exporting businesses, without allowing either consideration to obscure the other entirely.
Trade with China
China has been South Africa’s largest trading partner since 2008. Bilateral trade exceeded $34bn in 2023 and continued expanding through to the present. South African exports to China were estimated at $13.5bn in 2025, more than three times Agoa-supported exports. These figures suggest that the country’s broader growth prospects increasingly involve Asian demand and critical minerals.
Since the advent of Agoa in 2000, expanding Asian industrial production, commodity demand and infrastructure investment have shifted the economic centre of gravity eastward. Chinese customs data put two-way trade at $37.8bn in the first seven months of this year: about $21bn in imports from South Africa and $16bn in exports to South Africa. Despite methodological differences between the countries’ statistics, the figures point to deepening interdependence as relations with Washington becoming less certain.
Institutional ties have also strengthened. In 2026, South Africa and China signed the Framework Agreement on Economic Partnership for Shared Prosperity, followed by China’s unilateral zero-tariff arrangement for qualifying South African exports. These initiatives expand market access and provide a platform for deeper trade and investment.
Exports to China remain resource-intensive, dominated by gold, platinum group metals (PGMs), chrome, manganese and iron ore. Precious metals and stones account for 58% of the export basket, while ferro-alloy inputs, particularly chrome and manganese ores, contribute close to 29%.
Against those exports, South Africa imported about $22.9bn from China in 2025. The imbalance exposes dependence on raw material exports but also demonstrates the strategic fit between China’s industrial demand and South Africa’s mineral wealth.
China’s leading electric vehicle, battery, renewable energy equipment, steel and advanced manufacturing industries require manganese, chrome, vanadium, iron ore, copper, nickel and PGMs. South Africa’s globally significant reserves make it relevant to this next phase of China’s industrial development.
Stats SA’s GDP rebasing reinforces mining’s importance. The revised economy is about 5% larger than previously estimated, and mining accounted for the largest upward revision at 12.5%, reflecting improved measurement and broader coverage rather than new production. Mining and trade together accounted for R122bn of the R324bn upward GDP revision, highlighting the previously underestimated footprint of resource-linked activity.
Technological change strengthens this significance. Renewable energy, battery storage, electric mobility, AI infrastructure and advanced defence technologies are driving demand for strategic minerals. Governments increasingly regard secure supplies as essential to economic sovereignty and national security.
South Africa holds some of the world’s largest reserves of PGMs, manganese, chromium and vanadium and remains a significant gold producer. The policy response to Agoa’s termination must therefore go beyond finding alternative markets.
South Africa should leverage its mineral endowment to move up global value chains, treating industrialisation, and not extraction alone, as the central challenge. Exporting raw or semi-processed minerals while importing higher-value manufactures has restricted domestic value capture, a model increasingly inadequate for the critical-minerals era.
Beneficiation imperative
Beneficiation is therefore an economic imperative. Expanding domestic refining, processing and manufacturing could shift exports from manganese and chrome ores and platinum concentrates towards battery materials, speciality alloys, catalytic technologies, hydrogen components and fuel cells, thus deepening industrial capacity and reducing exposure to commodity cycles.
China could provide capital and expertise in battery technology, renewable energy and mineral processing. Moving from resource exports to industrial collaboration could make South Africa–China relations a defining economic partnership of the next decade.
The strategic objective should not be to replace dependence on Washington with dependence on Beijing. Larger trade flows alone cannot guarantee industrial transformation if South Africa continues exporting minerals while importing the finished products. Partnerships should therefore be judged by their contribution to local processing, technological capability and access to markets for higher-value exports.
Chinese capital and expertise would be most valuable when they support these outcomes, alongside co-operation with other trading partners. This approach would make mineral wealth a basis for greater economic agency, rather than simply a source of commodity earnings vulnerable to external demand.
Green hydrogen illustrates the opportunity. South Africa’s solar and wind resources, combined with the PGMs that are central to many hydrogen technologies, offer strong advantages. Appropriate policy and investment could turn these into an export industry supporting clean energy manufacturing ecosystems.
Geopolitical competition over critical minerals also creates leverage. Demand from the US, China, the EU and other industrial powers could help South Africa cultivate diversified partnerships, attract investment, and develop domestic industry.
The bottom line is that Agoa’s termination is a serious sectoral setback but it need not define South Africa’s economic future. If the country succeeds in turning mineral wealth and diversified partnerships into domestic industrial capabilities, prosperity will depend less on preferences granted abroad than on value created at home.
• Dr Tshitereke, an honorary professor at Unisa’s Thabo Mbeki School of Public & International Affairs, is chief of staff at the mineral & petroleum resources ministry.

articles.title: Nigeria-Korea trade hits $1.1bn as both countries seek diversification - Vanguard News
articles.summary: Nigeria-Korea trade hits $1.1bn as both countries seek diversification  Vanguard News
articles.full_text:
By Favour Ulebor, Abuja
The Republic of Korea has expressed its readiness to deepen trade and investment ties with Nigeria, targeting sectors such as manufacturing, agriculture, digital technology and maritime services beyond the traditional oil and gas trade.
The Korean Ambassador to Nigeria, Jeong Yo-an, disclosed this on Wednesday at a meeting with journalists in Abuja, saying expanding economic cooperation would boost bilateral trade, encourage local production and create employment opportunities in both countries.
He said trade between Nigeria and Korea reached approximately $1.1bn last year, making Nigeria one of Korea’s largest trading partners in Africa.
However, the ambassador noted that the existing trade structure, largely dominated by Nigerian oil and gas exports and Korean exports of automobiles, electronics and machinery, needed to become more diversified.
“Last year, our trade reached about 1.1 billion dollars. Nigeria remains one of Korea’s largest trading partners in Africa. But the shape of our trade must change. Today, Nigeria sells us mostly oil and gas. Korea sells mostly cars, electronics and machinery. We can do much more than that,” he said.
Jeong said the next phase of bilateral cooperation would focus on strengthening local production, including vehicle assembly, agricultural machinery for rice farmers, digital skills development and maritime services.
He added that Korea was interested in encouraging more Nigerian businesses to participate in bilateral trade while attracting Korean companies to invest in local manufacturing and other productive sectors.
The ambassador identified the beauty and cosmetics industry as another area offering significant opportunities, citing growing Nigerian interest in Korean skincare and cosmetic products.
According to him, Nigeria’s large youth population presents a considerable market for Korean beauty products and could position the country as a major destination for such products in Africa.
He said the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA), through its Lagos office, was available to connect Korean manufacturers with Nigerian importers and help local businesses identify potential buyers in Korea.
Jeong also disclosed that Nigerian buyers would have the opportunity to engage with Korean companies at the Korean pavilion during the Beauty West Africa exhibition scheduled for November 13.
On diplomatic relations, he said both countries were working to strengthen and economic cooperation following the Korea-Africa Summit in 2024 and the first Korea-Africa Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in June this year.
He added that Nigeria had offered to host the seventh session of the Nigeria-Korea Joint Commission in Abuja as part of efforts to advance bilateral engagement.
On development cooperation, the ambassador disclosed that approximately 2,000 Nigerian public officials had received training in Korea through the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA).
He said KOICA’s Smart School project had also reached 8,000 pupils and trained more than 300 teachers and school leaders.
According to him, KOICA, the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) had commenced work on the Abuja Centre for Entrepreneurship to support young Nigerians in developing business ideas and creating jobs.
He said Korea was equally supporting initiatives aimed at promoting green jobs, agricultural development, digital education and skills acquisition.
The ambassador further disclosed that Korea was working towards increasing its Official Development Assistance to $10bn by 2030, alongside plans to provide $14bn in export financing to support Korean companies investing in Africa.
On cultural exchanges, Jeong said the Korean Cultural Centre Nigeria had reached more than 300,000 people through its programmes, while this year’s Korean Film Festival attracted approximately 1,000 participants.
He pledged to extend cultural activities to more Nigerian cities and promote collaborations between young creatives in both countries.

articles.title: FG Takes ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme To North-Central, Seeks Increased Regional Trade - Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.summary: FG Takes ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme To North-Central, Seeks Increased Regional Trade  Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.full_text:
The Federal Government has reaffirmed its commitment to boosting regional economic integration and intra-African trade through the effective implementation of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS).
The commitment was reiterated at a sensitisation workshop on the ETLS for the North-Central geopolitical zone, in Lokoja, Kogi State.
The workshop, themed, “Harnessing the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme to Promote Nigeria’s Interregional Trade and Economic Growth,” brought together government officials, business operators, regulatory agencies and other stakeholders to explore opportunities for expanding regional trade.
In his keynote address, Kogi State Governor, Ahmed Usman Ododo, represented by his Deputy, Salifu Joel Oyibo, described the scheme as an opportunity to expand the state’s economic reach, attract investment and connect local production to markets across West Africa.
Ododo identified Kogi’s strategic location, agricultural and mineral resources, road network and ongoing infrastructure projects, including the proposed Ajaokuta Free Trade Zone, agro-processing zone and Kogi International Airport, as important drivers of industrial development.
Spokesperson, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, in a statement on Wednesday said he called for improved transportation infrastructure, stronger inter-state collaboration and the removal of barriers to legitimate cross-border trade, including multiple checkpoints, cumbersome documentation and inadequate transport facilities.
The governor also urged businesses in the North-Central region to improve product quality, packaging and certification to enhance their competitiveness in the ECOWAS market.
Earlier, the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, described the ETLS as a major instrument of Nigeria’s regional integration agenda, providing duty-free and quota-free access for approved products originating from ECOWAS member states.
He disclosed that about 3,500 Nigerian companies and 20,000 products had been registered under the scheme, noting that the figures remained below Nigeria’s productive capacity and trade potential.
Enikanolaiye called for increased awareness, stronger institutional coordination and deliberate efforts to address challenges limiting the scheme’s implementation.
He noted that Nigeria’s large population, market size, natural resources, entrepreneurial base and productive capacity positioned the country to play a significant role in advancing the ETLS and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The minister urged manufacturers, agricultural producers and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) to take advantage of the scheme, stressing that it aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy by 2030.
He also linked the initiative to Nigeria’s four-D foreign policy priorities of Demography, Development, Diaspora and Democracy, as well as the principle of strategic autonomy.
The minister encouraged Kogi State and other North-Central states to harness their agricultural, livestock and mineral resources through value addition and integrated industrial production to increase their participation in regional trade.
He further urged participants to understand the registration, certification and rules-of-origin requirements for accessing the ECOWAS market.
Other stakeholders, including the Secretary to the Kogi State Government, Pastor Mrs Fola Shadia Rekiya Iwade, reaffirmed the state’s readiness to support trade and investment through institutional assistance for MSMEs.
The organised private sector also called for the removal of non-tariff barriers and pledged to mobilise businesses, promote awareness of the scheme and support compliance with export requirements.
In his closing remarks, Enikanolaiye said the North-Central region possessed considerable untapped potential in agriculture, livestock, mining and manufacturing, capable of supporting Nigeria’s competitiveness across West Africa.
He stressed that regional integration should translate into practical economic benefits, including employment creation, increased income and improved livelihoods.
The minister urged businesses to register under the scheme, comply with applicable standards and documentation requirements, while calling on relevant Ministries, Departments and Agencies to provide exporters with timely and transparent institutional support without unnecessary bureaucratic delays.
He appreciated the Kogi State Government, ECOWAS Commission, resource persons, regulatory agencies, chambers of commerce and the business community for supporting the workshop.

articles.title: Four African countries unlock $675 million for energy, water and climate-resilient infrastructure expected to protect 4.5 million people - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Four African countries unlock $675 million for energy, water and climate-resilient infrastructure expected to protect 4.5 million people  Business Insider AfricaAFC, GCF launch US$690 million African climate finance facility  Africa Business Communities
articles.full_text:
- The Green Climate Fund has approved $274.96 million for Nigeria, Angola, Benin and Côte d’Ivoire.
- The funding forms part of a $674.88 million programme that includes $399.92 million in co-financing.
- Projects will cover electricity networks, renewable energy, food systems, water supply and climate-resilient infrastructure.
- The programme is expected to improve the resilience of 4.5 million people and avoid 3.4 million tonnes of emissions.
Angola, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria will receive financing through the Africa Sovereign Climate Facility, a programme managed by the Africa Finance Corporation.
The facility will help the four governments identify, prepare and finance projects designed to withstand floods, droughts, rising temperatures, unpredictable rainfall and other climate-related pressures.
According to the Green Climate Fund’s official project record, the programme has a total value of $674.88 million.
The global fund will provide $274.96 million, comprising approximately $255.32 million in loans and $19.64 million in grants. Another $399.92 million will be provided through co-financing.
Africa Finance Corporation separately described the package as a $690 million facility in its announcement. It said the Green Climate Fund’s contribution was about $280 million, while it would arrange and fully fund a parallel commercial facility of up to $260 million.
However, the Green Climate Fund’s approved project page provides the more precise figures, listing $674.88 million as the total project value and $274.96 million as its own contribution.
Energy, water and food projects targeted
The financing will be channelled through the ministries of finance in the four participating countries.
Eligible investments include electricity transmission, distribution and storage systems, renewable-energy access, water supply, sanitation, food systems and infrastructure designed to withstand climate-related shocks.
Some of the grant funding will finance technical assistance. This will help governments develop investment-ready projects, integrate climate risks into economic and fiscal planning and improve project monitoring.
The facility is expected to increase the climate resilience of approximately 4.5 million people and avoid about 3.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over its lifetime.
The Green Climate Fund approved the programme on 28 October 2026. Its implementation had not commenced at the time the project record was published.
Africa Finance Corporation President and Chief Executive Officer Samaila Zubairu said the programme would help governments convert national development priorities into reliable energy, stronger food and water systems and more resilient infrastructure.
“The infrastructure we build today must both power Africa’s growth and withstand the climate pressures of tomorrow,” he said.
The programme responds to a persistent financing challenge across African economies. Governments face growing infrastructure and climate-adaptation needs but often pay high borrowing costs and have limited fiscal space to fund long-term projects.
The participating countries are also exposed to different combinations of coastal flooding, drought, extreme heat, erratic rainfall and pressure on food and water systems.
By combining concessional funding with commercial loans, the facility is intended to lower financing risks and create projects capable of attracting additional capital.
The new programme builds on an earlier partnership between the Green Climate Fund and Africa Finance Corporation. In 2023, the climate fund committed $253 million to an AFC-managed infrastructure fund targeting climate-resilient assets across Africa.

articles.title: Uganda’s Industrial Sector Contributes 24.9% of GDP as Gov’t Targets $500 Billion Economy - ChimpReports
articles.summary: Uganda’s Industrial Sector Contributes 24.9% of GDP as Gov’t Targets $500 Billion Economy  ChimpReports
articles.full_text:
The sector recorded annual growth of 6.4% in 2025 and has expanded from 81 industries in 1986 to more than 12,000 formal manufacturing industries, Trade, Industry and Cooperatives Minister Sanjay Tanna said on Wednesday.
Speaking at the launch of the National Industrialization Conference 2026 at Uganda Media Centre, Tanna said industrialisation was central to the government’s Ten-Fold Growth Strategy, which seeks to expand the economy from its current size towards $500 billion.
“The private sector remains the primary engine of growth, while Government is committed to creating an enabling environment that promotes investment, innovation, enterprise development and competitiveness,” Tanna said.
He said manufacturing consumed more than 70% of Uganda’s electricity generation, while manufactured exports accounted for 24.6% of total merchandise exports in 2025.
Uganda’s economy has grown from $3.9 billion in 1986 to $61.9 billion in 2025, while gross national income per capita has risen to $1,389, placing the country above the current threshold for lower-middle-income economies, according to Tanna.
Exports of goods and services increased by 204%, from $5.93 billion in 2022 to $18.04 billion in 2026, driven by gold, coffee, cocoa, sugar, fish and manufactured products.
Exports from free zones reached $1.37 billion, while foreign direct investment stood at $3.2 billion.
Tanna said Uganda had become a net exporter of several products it previously imported, including soap, sugar, milk, salt, cooking oil, soda, beer, cement, steel and paper.
“In the past 15 years we have added over 31 new value-added products to our export basket,” he said.
The products include ceramic tiles, leather, processed foods, dairy products, electric transformers, electric meters, textiles, apparel and pharmaceuticals.
The government has identified agro-based industries, extractive industries and knowledge-intensive manufacturing as priority areas for industrial development.
Under its industrialisation programme, Uganda has established eight operational industrial parks out of 22 planned across the country. The parks have attracted investments worth $5.8 billion and created more than 163,010 jobs.
Tanna said the government was prioritising increased value addition to local raw materials, with investments targeting iron and steel, cement, phosphates, copper, packaging, pharmaceuticals, starch, sugar and textiles.
The government is also seeking to reduce production costs through infrastructure investment, access to finance and lower electricity tariffs for industrial users.
Electricity tariffs for high-energy industrial consumers have been reduced to 5.7 US cents per kilowatt-hour, while resources have been earmarked to improve transmission infrastructure and power reliability.
On industrial financing, Tanna said the Uganda Development Bank (UDB) had cumulative capital of about 1.6 trillion shillings, while the Uganda Development Corporation (UDC) had a target of 5 trillion shillings in capitalisation within five years.
The government is also implementing the Buy Uganda Build Uganda policy to support local manufacturers and pursuing access to regional and continental markets through the East African Community, Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa and African Continental Free Trade Area.
The AfCFTA provides access to a continental market of approximately 1.4 billion people, with a combined GDP exceeding $3 trillion, Tanna said.
The minister announced that the National Industrialization Conference 2026 will take place in Kampala from November 18 to 20 under the theme “Celebrating Uganda’s Industrial Growth”.
The conference is being organised by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Cooperatives in partnership with UDC and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO).
It will bring together policymakers, investors, manufacturers, researchers and other industry stakeholders to discuss investment, domestic manufacturing, value addition and job creation.
“The primary objective of the Conference is to bring together policymakers, industry leaders, investors, and researchers to translate national economic goals into practical manufacturing growth, policy implementation, and investment,” Tanna said.
The conference will also coincide with the commemoration of Africa Industrialization Day on November 20 and mark the 10th anniversary of the re-establishment of UDC in 2016.
Tanna said the event would provide an opportunity to showcase Uganda’s productive capacity, mobilise investment, expand market access and promote technology adoption.
He called on the business community to participate in the conference and take advantage of investment and market opportunities to support the country’s industrial transformation.

articles.summary: GDP Rebasing to Lay Foundation for Ethiopia’s Long-Term Dev’t Ambitions: Minister  ENA English

GDP Rebasing to Lay Foundation for Ethiopia’s Long-Term Dev’t Ambitions: Minister
Addis Ababa, November 4, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia’s newly completed Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rebasing will provide a stronger foundation for the country’s long-term development ambitions, particularly its vision of building a prosperous nation, Minister of National Strategy Bereket Fesehatsion said.
Ethiopia today unveiled its updated GDP figures as part of efforts to modernize economic measurement and reflect structural changes in the economy.
With the 2017 Ethiopian fiscal year (2024/25) as the new base year, the country’s GDP reached 24.03 trillion Birr (201.42 billion USD).
The figure further rose to 31.86 trillion Birr (210.7 billion USD) in the 2018 Ethiopian fiscal year (2025/26).
Speaking at the launch of the updated GDP rebasing results, Minister Bereket said the revised measurement system provides a more accurate picture of the country's economic structure by incorporating emerging economic activities and previously underrepresented sectors.
He noted that the updated economic structure underscores the importance of moving beyond quantitative growth toward building a productive economy.
He pointed out that the new GDP rebasing would help generate employment, strengthen domestic production capacity, and reduce excessive dependence on primary commodities.
The minister further emphasized that reliable economic statistics are essential for improving policy formulation, budget allocation, investment decisions, and economic planning, while strengthening the confidence of domestic and international investors.
He said the revised GDP framework would provide a more accurate benchmark for assessing national economic objectives, including foreign trade, revenue generation, investment, and employment creation.
The 2017 Ethiopian fiscal year, corresponding to 2024/25 in the Gregorian calendar, was selected as the new base year for the exercise, taking into account its relative macroeconomic stability, declining inflation, and the availability of comprehensive statistical data.
The process incorporated findings from the agricultural census, the economic establishments census, and household surveys, among other sources, enabling the country to update its national accounts in line with contemporary economic realities.
The minister stated that the exercise was conducted under the leadership of Ethiopian professionals, with technical assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), to ensure alignment with the 2008 System of National Accounts and other international standards.
He also highlighted the government's efforts to strengthen national statistical capacity by recruiting and training young graduates to work alongside experienced professionals, ensuring the transfer of technical knowledge and the sustainability of the process.
The government will institutionalize GDP rebasing every five years to maintain the reliability and relevance of national economic statistics, it was indicated.
The minister said the updated measurement system would serve as a new foundation for Ethiopia's long-term development ambitions, particularly its vision of building a prosperous country by 2050 through strengthened domestic capacity and improved living standards for citizens.

articles.summary: Unions urge South Africa to save US duty-free trade deal  France 24
articles.full_text:
Johannesburg (AFP) – South African unions urged the government Tuesday to work to save a US duty-free trade deal that supports thousands of jobs, while analysts played down the broader economic impact.
Issued on:
Washington announced Monday that from January 1 South Africa and Rwanda would be removed from the Africa-US trade preference programme granted to several countries.
About 10 percent of South African exports to the United States in 2025 entered under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) programme, which mainly covers the agriculture, manufacturing and automobile sectors.
The country's largest trade union federation, Cosatu, told AFP that between 3,000 and 10,000 agriculture and manufacturing jobs could be on the line.
Some of the companies most at risk are based in small towns, for example the citrus-producing areas of the Western Cape province, said Cosatu representative Matthew Parks.
"There's a danger of creating ghost towns," he said.
"We are meeting with government to encourage them to go to the US, use the next 60 days to negotiate a possible package deal," Parks said.
The Citrus Growers' Association of Southern Africa warned Monday that jobs and the economies of entire towns were at stake.
Strained diplomatic ties
South Africa is the largest beneficiary of AGOA, which grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the US market.
The deal has been renewed until the end of 2028 but South Africa and Rwanda were given notice of their removal after an annual review that cited "concerning" practices.
These include "barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests", a US statement said.
Pretoria had been prepared for exclusion because of its battered diplomatic ties with Washington over various domestic and international policy differences.
For the automobile sector, "the most severe blow" had been the Trump administration's 25-percent tariffs imposed in April 2025, said the Motor Industry Staff Association (MISA) union.
As a result, South African vehicle exports to the United States plunged by 83 percent to 4,136 units in 2025, it said in a statement.
"Government must make full use of the 60-day notice period because the possibility of reinstatement remains," it said, also calling for an "automotive trade solution".
"While the decision is significant and disappointing, it does not amount to a trade ban. South African vehicles will continue to be sold in the American market," MISA said.
International relations expert Kingsley Makhubela said it would be a "waste of time" for South Africa to appeal its removal.
"It's a political decision that has been made by the Trump administration; it's not a trade decision," he told AFP.
Makhubela said 134,000 jobs could be directly impacted, significant in an economy with an official unemployment rate running above 30 percent.
But Daryl Swanepoel, from the independent Inclusive Society Institute (ISI) policy research group, said claims of massive job losses were "alarmist" and assumed South African products would not be sold at all, which was not the case.
The United States will still need certain imports, for example citrus, even though they will be more expensive to consumers, he told AFP.
Minerals -- a major South African export -- remains exempted, he said, estimating the loss of AGOA would impact GDP by less than one percent.
"I believe the South African economy is mature enough to deal with this," Swanepoel said.
Removal from the duty-free deal "does not mean that all South African exports to the US will suddenly face new tariffs or disappear," said economist Johann Els, from PSG Financial Services.
While AGOA covered 10 percent of South African exports to the United States, this was just 0.7 percent of the country's total exports, he said in a statement.
"So, while the absolute numbers may look significant, the share of our overall exports directly affected is relatively small," he said.

articles.title: US decision to boot South Africa from trade deal slammed as devastating blow to economy - https://novanews.co.za/
articles.summary: US decision to boot South Africa from trade deal slammed as devastating blow to economy  https://novanews.co.za/
articles.full_text:
South Africa has accused the United States of raising “new issues” after President Donald Trump announced plans to kick the country out of a duty-free trade agreement, a move the government says will badly hurt the economy.
Trump notified Congress on Monday of his intention to end South Africa’s eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective from 1 January 2027. The decision gives the country 60 days before the proposed termination takes effect.
Trade Minister Parks Tau said Washington was introducing concerns that had not previously been part of negotiations that began in 2025, despite Pretoria offering extra concessions.
“It is however unfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions as part of the negotiations process that commenced in 2025,” Tau said in a statement on Monday.
The minister acknowledged the impact on workers, exporters and businesses but said the government would support affected industries.
“AGOA remains important to South Africa, but it does not constitute the totality of the economic relationship between South Africa and the United States,” he said.
Why the US is cutting South Africa from AGOA
The US Trade Representative said an interagency review found South African practices inconsistent with AGOA eligibility requirements.
Washington cited five key concerns:
- Barriers to US trade and investment in South Africa
- Corruption
- Threats to US national security interests
- Threats to US foreign policy interests
- Allegations of discrimination against white Afrikaners, which South Africa rejects as false
The US statement did not specify individual corruption cases or particular foreign relationships but comes as the Trump administration has stepped up criticism of Pretoria’s alignment with Russia and Iran.
AGOA was established in May 2000 as an act of economic goodwill to help grow South Africa’s post-apartheid economy. The scheme’s rigorous eligibility requirements include continual progress towards a market-based economy and a commitment to the rule of law.
Economic impact on key sectors
The decision affects exporters relying on preferential access to the US market. South Africa is the scheme’s largest beneficiary, though the economic exposure has already declined sharply.
About 28% of South African exports to the US entered under AGOA in 2024, worth about $4 billion (R72 billion). This dropped to about 10% in 2025, worth about $1.7 billion (R30.6 billion).
The programme provides duty-free access to the US market for South African vehicles, the country’s second-largest export earner to the United States after precious metals, according to the South African Revenue Service.
Agriculture and agro-processing, automotive manufacturing, and mining sectors face the biggest hit. Hundreds of thousands of South Africans employed through AGOA-dependent industries are now at risk.
The exclusion also affects Rwanda, adding to uncertainty for African exporters who have relied on the preferential trade terms.
Political backlash and blame game
The Democratic Alliance (DA) has blamed the exclusion on what it called the ANC’s “diplomatic ineptitude” and failed foreign policy.
DA spokesperson on international relations Ryan Smith said the development was avoidable and completely unnecessary in the context of sound economic diplomacy.
“This decision is a devastating blow to the South African economy, especially the agriculture and agro-processing, automotive manufacturing, and mining sectors,” Smith said.
“Hundreds of thousands of South Africans employed through AGOA-dependent industries will now pay the price for Minister Lamola’s ideological obstinacy and sheer diplomatic ineptitude.”
Smith blamed International Relations Minister Lamola for failing to protect South Africa’s economic interests with the USA, the country’s second-largest trading partner.
“As our country’s chief diplomat, Minister Lamola is tasked with placing the interests of South African citizens ahead of party-political whims,” he said.
The DA also pointed to what it described as the ANC’s alignment with “international despots and human rights abusers in Russia and Iran” as damaging South Africa’s standing with liberal democracies.
Freedom Front Plus (FF Plus) leader Dr Corne Mulder said the ANC had been warned repeatedly about the consequences of its foreign policy choices.
“The ANC and President Ramaphosa are wholly to blame for AGOA disaster and economic consequences,” Mulder said in a media statement.
The FF Plus said it and other organisations had visited Washington several times to argue that ordinary South Africans should not be punished for ANC foreign policy and that South Africa should not be removed from AGOA.
The party claimed the ANC threatened parties that advocated South Africa’s case internationally with prosecution, including possible high-treason charges.
ALSO READ: Ramaphosa warns South Africa to brace for US trade deal exit
COSATU general secretary Solly Mapaila took a different view, blaming lobby groups AfriForum and Solidarity for helping strain South Africa-US relations.
“They should explain the consequences to affected farmers and workers,” Mapaila said on 3 November.
South Africa’s cabinet had welcomed an August extension of AGOA through 31 December 2028, which would have maintained preferential access for eligible South African products. The November action is therefore a proposed country-specific termination despite that broader extension.
Minister Tau said AGOA exports represented roughly 1% of South Africa’s total global exports in 2025, with about 89% of exports to the US entering under ordinary World Trade Organisation most-favoured-nation terms.
The proposed termination will take effect on 1 January unless the process is reversed or otherwise resolved through diplomatic channels.
