articles.title: US to exclude South Africa, Rwanda from Africa duty-free trade deal - www.standardmedia.co.ke
articles.summary: US to exclude South Africa, Rwanda from Africa duty-free trade deal  www.standardmedia.co.ke
articles.full_text:
The United States said on Monday it would remove South Africa and Rwanda from a major Africa-US trade preference programme, citing practices it said were "inconsistent" with the scheme's eligibility criteria.
"These concerning and pervasive practices include, but are not limited to, barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region," Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.
                            
The exclusions will take effect from January 1, the statement said.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the US market, has been renewed until the end of 2028, but is reviewed annually.
South Africa is the program's largest beneficiary, but its eligibility has come under scrutiny as Washington steps up criticism of Pretoria, including false allegations of discrimination against white Afrikaners that South Africa rejects.
                            
Trade Minister Parks Tau said it was "unfortunate" that Washington was raising issues that had not previously featured in negotiations, despite additional concessions offered by Pretoria.
Acknowledging the potential fallout for workers and businesses, Tau said the government had retained measures introduced in response to US reciprocal tariffs and would support affected industries while stepping up efforts to diversify export markets.
"AGOA remains important to South Africa, but it does not constitute the totality of the economic relationship between South Africa and the United States," he said.
About 10 per cent of South African exports to the US entered under the programme in 2025, down from 28 per cent in the previous year, he said.
                            
The programme provides duty-free access to the US market for South African vehicles, the country's second-largest export earner to the United States after precious metals, according to the South African Revenue Service.
- 'Serious blow' for citrus growers -
The Citrus Growers' Association of Southern Africa (CGA) called the exclusion "a serious blow" to the industry, warning that jobs and the economies of entire towns were at stake.
South Africa is the world's second-largest citrus exporter after Spain, and citrus is its largest agricultural export sector by value.
                            
Growers cannot easily redirect fruit to alternative markets because importing countries have different phytosanitary requirements and consumer preferences, said Gerrit van der Merwe, the association's chairman.
"That entire value chain, on both sides of the Atlantic, is now under threat," CGA said in a statement.
The US president reviews countries' eligibility for AGOA annually.
Any removal requires 60 days' notice to Congress and the country concerned.
Washington has also been increasing economic pressure on Rwanda over its alleged backing of the armed M23 rebel group in neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
Last week, the United States sanctioned the Rwandan defence ministry over those ties, which the Rwandan government denies.
With Rwandan help, the M23 movement has seized swathes of the eastern DRC -- home to valuable minerals coveted by world powers -- since it took up arms again in 2021.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe told AFP last week that his country should not be a "scapegoat" for events in DR Congo.
"The situation in the DRC, the political situation, the security situation, is mainly a Congolese issue," Nduhungirehe told AFP on the sidelines of a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow before the US sanctions were imposed.
"Rwanda must not be held as a scapegoat for what is happening in Congo forever," he added.

articles.title: FG targets West African market for Nigerian businesses through ECOWAS trade scheme - Business News Nigeria
articles.summary: FG targets West African market for Nigerian businesses through ECOWAS trade scheme  Business News Nigeria
articles.full_text:
The Federal Government is seeking to expand Nigerian businesses’ access to the West African market through the effective implementation of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS).
This was as it moves to address low business participation and barriers limiting regional trade.
The government said only about 3,500 Nigerian companies and 20,000 products had been registered under the scheme, a figure it considers significantly below the country’s productive capacity and potential to benefit from duty-free and quota-free access to markets across the West African sub-region.
Sola Enikanolaiye, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, disclosed this at a sensitisation workshop on the ETLS for the North-Central geopolitical zone held on Monday in Lokoja, Kogi State.
The workshop, organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, was themed, “Harnessing the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme to Promote Nigeria’s Interregional Trade and Economic Growth.”
Enikanolaiye described the ETLS as a cornerstone of Nigeria’s regional integration agenda, designed to promote trade among ECOWAS member states by granting approved products originating from member countries duty-free and quota-free access to the regional market.
He said the scheme was established to strengthen economic cooperation, stimulate industrial growth and support micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), but its benefits remained largely untapped because of inadequate awareness, institutional coordination gaps and difficulties navigating registration and certification requirements.
The minister called for increased participation by manufacturers, agricultural producers and MSMEs, stressing that Nigerian businesses needed to take advantage of the regional market to expand production, attract investment and improve their competitiveness.
The low level of registration comes despite Nigeria’s significant economic influence in West Africa, supported by its large population, market size, natural resources, entrepreneurial base and productive capacity.
According to the minister, these advantages position the country to play a leading role in advancing the objectives of both the ETLS and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which are intended to deepen trade liberalisation, regional economic integration and sustainable development.
He linked greater participation in the scheme to President Bola Tinubu’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy by 2030, noting that expanding access to regional markets would create opportunities for Nigerian producers to scale operations and increase economic output.
Enikanolaiye also connected the scheme to Nigeria’s foreign policy priorities, known as the 4Ds, Demography, Development, Diaspora and Democracy and the principle of strategic autonomy, which places national interests and the welfare of Nigerians at the centre of the country’s diplomatic engagements.
He urged businesses in Kogi and other North-Central states to move beyond the production of raw commodities by investing in value addition and integrated industrial production, particularly in agriculture, livestock and mineral resources.
Such investments, he said, would strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to compete in the West African market while enabling local businesses to benefit from the opportunities provided by the trade liberalisation scheme.
The minister also urged participants to use the workshop to understand the scheme’s registration procedures, product certification requirements and rules of origin, which determine whether goods qualify for preferential treatment under the ETLS.
Ahmed Usman Ododo, Governor of Kogi State, represented by Salifu Oyibo, his deputy, said the scheme presented an opportunity for the state to expand its economic reach, attract investments and connect local production to markets across West Africa.
He identified Kogi’s strategic geographical location, agricultural and mineral resources, road network and ongoing infrastructure projects as important assets that could support industrial development and increased regional trade.
The governor specifically highlighted the proposed Ajaokuta Free Trade Zone, agro-processing zone and Kogi International Airport as projects capable of improving the state’s economic prospects and creating new opportunities for businesses.
However, he said the ability of Kogi businesses to benefit from regional trade would depend partly on addressing infrastructure and administrative constraints that increase the cost and difficulty of moving goods across state and national borders.
He called for improved transportation infrastructure, stronger collaboration among states and the removal of barriers to legitimate cross-border trade.
These barriers, he said, include multiple checkpoints, inadequate transportation facilities, cumbersome documentation procedures and limited access to trade-related information.
Ododo reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to creating an enabling environment for investment and enterprise development, while urging businesses in the North-Central region to improve product quality, packaging and certification to meet requirements in the ECOWAS market.
Fola Iwade, Secretary to the Kogi State Government, also reaffirmed the state’s readiness to support trade and investment through institutional assistance and business facilitation, particularly for MSMEs.
Stakeholders at the workshop further identified transportation and logistics infrastructure as critical to unlocking the region’s trade potential, calling for improvements in rail networks, inland waterways and cargo-handling facilities to facilitate the movement of goods to domestic and international markets.
The organised private sector also called for the removal of non-tariff barriers, while pledging to mobilise businesses, increase awareness of the ETLS and support companies in meeting export requirements.
In his closing remarks, Enikanolaiye said the North-Central region possessed substantial but underutilised resources in agriculture, livestock, solid minerals and manufacturing that could compete beyond Nigeria’s domestic market.
He noted that although businesses, particularly MSMEs, were willing to explore regional trade opportunities, many required clearer information, stronger institutional support and simpler procedures to participate legitimately and competitively.
The minister stressed that regional economic integration should not be treated merely as a diplomatic undertaking but as a practical instrument for creating jobs, increasing incomes and improving livelihoods.
He urged businesses to take concrete steps to register under the scheme, comply with applicable product standards and documentation requirements, and position their products to benefit from preferential access to the ECOWAS market.
He also called on relevant ministries, departments and agencies to provide exporters with timely, transparent and efficient institutional support, warning against unnecessary bureaucratic delays that could undermine businesses’ ability to access regional markets.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs reaffirmed its commitment to working with the ECOWAS Commission, regulatory agencies, chambers of commerce and industry and the private sector to translate the opportunities offered by the ETLS into measurable economic benefits for Nigerian businesses.

articles.title: Nation's new demand opens trade opportunities for Africa - China Daily Global Edition
articles.summary: Nation's new demand opens trade opportunities for Africa  China Daily Global Edition
articles.full_text:
Nation's new demand opens trade opportunities for Africa
By Carlos Lopes | China Daily | Updated: 2026-11-05 09:26
When the 9th China International Import Expo opens in Shanghai on Thursday, the most consequential question for African exporters will not simply be how much China is prepared to buy. It will be what a changing Chinese economy will need to buy in the years ahead. Understanding that distinction could transform the economic relationship between China and Africa.
For more than two decades, China's demand for oil, metals and other raw materials helped sustain African commodity exports, and Chinese manufacturing supplied African markets with machinery, equipment and consumer goods. This relationship contributed to the economic growth of both sides.
Now the Chinese economy is shifting toward a different demand mix. Technological upgrading, the energy transition, demographic change and the expansion of services are reshaping consumption and production. The emphasis of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) is on domestic consumption, technological innovation and higher-quality growth. Its ambition to expand retail sales to about 60 trillion yuan ($9 trillion) by 2030 underscores the importance of a stronger domestic market.
For African economies, this deserves as much attention as the traditional indicators of Chinese industrial output, as it offers new opportunities.
The first opportunity concerns changing consumer preferences. Rising demand for differentiated food products, healthier diets, specialty agricultural goods and higher-quality consumer experiences creates possibilities for African producers well beyond traditional commodity exports. Coffee from Ethiopia and Kenya, cocoa products from West Africa, horticultural exports, fruit, seafood and processed foods can reach increasingly sophisticated Chinese consumers.
But capturing these opportunities requires more than just expanding agricultural production. It demands investment in processing, certification, traceability, cold chains, branding and distribution. African exporters must become more familiar with Chinese consumer preferences and digital retail platforms. The objective should not simply be to sell more cocoa beans, for example, but to participate in the higher-value segments of the chocolate and confectionery industries.
China's decision to extend zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations, effective May 1,2026, provides an important opening. At a time when protectionism is increasing elsewhere, this initiative sends a welcome signal about market access.
To fully realize this potential, continued efforts to strengthen logistics, improve product quality and certification, and enhance African exporters' understanding of the Chinese market will be important. Closer cooperation in these areas can help more African businesses benefit from the expanded market access.
The second opportunity arises from China's changing industrial structure.
As Chinese enterprises move toward more technologically sophisticated activities, evolving industrial structures, rising competitive intensity and changing global trade conditions are encouraging greater internationalization of production. Africa offers possibilities for investment in light manufacturing, agro-processing, renewable-energy equipment, batteries and electric mobility, with potential to strengthen local production capacity and regional value chains.
This should not be understood merely as relocating low-cost production. Africa's growing population, expanding urban markets and increasing demand for energy and digital technologies create opportunities to combine local manufacturing with access to regional markets.
The African Continental Free Trade Area could be particularly important in this regard. Rather than treating individual African countries as relatively small markets, Chinese investors could build production networks that serve a much larger continental economy. Such investments would also support the industrial diversification African governments have repeatedly sought through the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation.
The third opportunity concerns the evolution of Chinese demand for minerals and energy inputs.
China's technological upgrading and green transition will sustain demand for copper, lithium, cobalt, graphite and other strategic materials. However, Africa's development opportunity lies less in exporting greater volumes of unprocessed minerals than in capturing more of the associated value chains.
Processing, refining, component manufacturing and technological cooperation should increasingly become part of the investment proposition. China's considerable expertise in industrial ecosystems could help African economies overcome constraints that individual investments cannot resolve.
Bilateral merchandise trade reached approximately $348 billion in 2025. During the first eight months of 2026, Chinese imports from Africa increased by 19 percent, demonstrating the continuing strength of Chinese demand.
China's evolving demand presents considerable opportunities for African economies to expand and diversify their exports. By developing new products, expanding processing and moving up the value chain, African countries can make better use of China's expanding market and deepen mutually beneficial trade and economic cooperation.
A more sustainable relationship will require African exports to become increasingly diversified, processed and technologically sophisticated. It will also require Chinese companies to see Africa not only as a source of inputs and a destination for exports, but as a location for investment, innovation and production. The most promising future for China-Africa trade is not simply one in which China imports more from Africa. It is one in which China's changing demand helps Africa produce differently, export more competitively and capture a greater share of the value generated by its own resources and capabilities.
The author is a former UN under-secretary-general and executive secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa, and now an honorary professor at the Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance, University of Cape Town.
The views do not necessarily reflect those of China Daily.
